articles.title: Eleições nos EUA: Políticos brasileiros repercutem vitória democrata | G1
articles.standfirst: Aliados de Lula classificaram eleições legislativas como 'derrota para Trump'. Direitista Renan Santos disse que governo dos EUA 'traiu' eleitores e tomou uma 'taca'.
articles.summary: Lideranças ligadas ao governo Lula e nomes da direita repercutem as eleições nos EUA após o Partido Democrata conquistar o controle do Congresso americano.
articles.body:
Políticos brasileiros, em especial lideranças ligadas ao governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ), se manifestaram nesta quarta-feira (4) sobre o desfecho das eleições de meio de mandato , as "midterms", nos Estados Unidos .

Realizada na terça-feira (3), a votação garantiu ao Partido Democrata o controle das duas Casas do Congresso americano — a Câmara dos Representantes e o Senado. O resultado configura uma derrota política para o presidente Donald Trump , do Partido Republicano.

Com o novo cenário, os democratas assumem o controle da pauta legislativa em Washington pelos próximos dois anos, impondo desafios e freios à gestão republicana.

O Palácio do Planalto não divulgou pronunciamento oficial sobre os resultados. Nem o presidente Lula nem o vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin comentaram a vitória democrata até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Integrantes da base governista e ministros comemoraram a virada legislativa em Washington e traçaram paralelos com a política nacional.

O ministro da Secretaria de Relações Institucionais (SRI), José Guimarães, disse que as eleições americanas apontam para uma "mudança de rumo" no mundo.

"Um verdadeiro tsunami americano varreu os EUA. Mudança de rumo no mundo que começou com a onda vermelha aqui no Brasil. Derrota de Trump é uma vitória do mundo democrático. Viva a Democracia", escreveu o ministro em sua conta no X.

O deputado André Janones ( Rede -MG), coordenador do canal "Exército do Lula" na campanha da reeleição do presidente, disse ver influência do cenário brasileiro no pelito dos EUA.

"A realidade é que a vitória do presidente Lula está inspirando o mundo inteiro. A gente tá mostrando pro mundo que, sim, nós podemos vencê-los de uma vez por todas", publicou o parlamentar.

Já o líder do governo no Congresso, senador Randolfe Rodrigues (PT-AP), ironizou ao parafrasear um bordão comumente adotado por setores conservadores. "Acontece no Brasil, acontece nos EUA. No final, quem interferiu fomos nós", postou Randolfe.

O deputado Lindbergh Farias (PT-RJ) usou a hashtag "TheBolsonarosEffect", que, em português, significa "o efeito Bolsonaro", e afirmou que as urnas mandaram um recado contra o avanço de grupos radicais.

"Derrota acachapante de Trump mostra que os EUA e o mundo estão dispostos a impedir que a extrema-direita destrua o nosso futuro", declarou o petista.

Paulo Teixeira, deputado do PT eleito por São Paulo, afirmou que, na sua avaliação, "os escândalos do governo Trump agora serão investigados".

O presidente nacional do PSB , João Campos , disse que a votação é uma resposta aos excessos e à radicalização do governo republicano.

"O recado das urnas ultrapassou o Congresso e chegou a redutos históricos republicanos: Gina Hinojosa, primeira governadora latina do Texas; Keisha Lance Bottoms, primeira mulher negra eleita governadora dos EUA, na Geórgia; e Rob Sand, vencedor em Iowa", citou Campos.

"Mais do que uma derrota de Trump, o resultado revela a formação de uma maioria diversa, que rejeita a política do confronto permanente e reafirma a força da democracia. Uma mensagem que ultrapassa as fronteiras americanas", completou o ex-prefeito do Recife (PE).

A deputada Duda Salabert ( PDT -MG) também destacou os marcos de representatividade nas urnas americanas e a contenção de alas de extrema-direita.

"Trump perdeu o controle do Congresso nos EUA, e as eleições de meio de mandato foram marcadas por conquistas históricas: primeira mulher indígena eleita para o Senado; primeira governadora negra da história dos EUA, na Geórgia; primeiro senador muçulmano eleito; primeira governadora indígena, no Novo México; primeiro senador abertamente gay", elencou Duda Salabert.

"Os resultados representam uma mudança na correlação de forças políticas nos EUA e uma reação eleitoral ao facismo de Trump. Estamos presenciando o fim da era do retrocesso", complementou a parlamentar.

O ex-candidato a presidente e líder do Partido Missão, Renan Santos , criticou tanto a condução dos EUA pelo governo Trump quanto a aproximação dos republicanos com o grupo do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro.

"Essa desgraça de direita retardada dos republicanos, que tem, nos Bolsonaro, sua filial, tomaram uma taca. Que acabem logo. Trump toca um governo essencialmente corrupto que traiu seus eleitores. Que surja algo novo no lugar", afirmou Renan em uma rede social.

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, discursa durante um comício de campanha para as eleições de meio de mandato, no Ocean Center, em Daytona Beach, na Flórida, em 30 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP

articles.title: Marsha Blackburn makes history as the first woman elected Tennessee governor
articles.summary: U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn is set to be the state’s 51st governor, making history as the first woman to hold that office.
articles.body:
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn made history Nov. 3, becoming the first woman elected to serve as Tennessee's governor, NBC News and Decision Desk HQ projected.

"My promise is pretty simple: Tennessee is going to be a state where hard work pays off, where families can put down roots, and where everyone has the opportunity to build a better future," she told supporters in Nashville.

Blackburn said her campaign's grassroots approach helped propel her to victory.

"We ran a different kind of campaign, focused on Tennesseans, not on the media's terms and not on any other candidate's terms," Blackburn said. "We ran a campaign that was for the people of Tennessee, and we have proved that this is how you win. You build a campaign from the grassroots, from the bottom up, not the top down."

Blackburn will succeed fellow Republican Gov. Bill Lee, who is term limited after eight years in office.

"Congratulations to Governor-Elect Marsha Blackburn on her victory," Lee said in a statement. "Tennesseans have placed their trust in a conservative leader who understands the importance of fiscal responsibility, keeping communities safe, and creating opportunities for every family to thrive.

"Conservative leadership has positioned Tennessee to lead the nation as a beacon of opportunity, security, and freedom, and Tennesseans have made clear that they want to see that momentum continue.

"I look forward to working with Governor-Elect Blackburn in the coming months to ensure a smooth transition and continued prosperity for our state."

Country music from the band The Austin Brothers filled the venue as Blackburn's supporters awaited election results . Some supporters wore red caps with "MARSHA" emblazoned on them.

"Tennessee has become a Christian conservative standard-bearer, and it is the place that people want to be," Blackburn said in her victory speech. "So our job is going to be to keep what we've got and to make the best better."

Democratic nominee Jerri Green conceded in the race in Chattanooga just after 10:30 p.m. CT.

Green took the stage with her family and campaign team as the crowd chanted "Jerri! Jerri! Jerri!" She told the crowd that while the votes were not yet completely counted, she did not see a path to victory.

"Tonight, I didn't win for you," Green said.

"I want you to know something, Tennessee: I'm not going anywhere – and I hope you aren't either," Green said, giving her youngest son, Wilder, a hug. "The future of this state is my flesh and blood, so I am not done fighting."

She thanked her team and her supporters for making the race "us as close as we've been in decades."

Unofficial results from the Tennessee Secretary of State show Blackburn captured about 45.5% of the vote, Green 42.9%. Fewer than 55,000 votes separated them.

No Tennessee governor has won with less than 50% of the vote in at least the last century. Gov. Phil Bredesen won with 50.65% in 2002, and Gov. Frank Clement won with 50.9% in 1962.

Independent candidate David Hatley conceded the governor's race shortly after 9 p.m. ET at his event in Johnson City. While he earned less than 10% of the vote, Hatley vastly overperformed independent candidates, who in recent decades have struggled to break 2% of the vote.

Hatley initially meant to run as a Republican. But because of a federal bank fraud charge he pleaded guilty to in 1998, he had not voted in enough recent Republican primary elections to qualify for the Republican ballot.

Instead, he ran as an independent, pouring $12 million of his personal fortune into his bid.

Hatley aligned with Republicans on issues like book bans , tax cuts and abortion, but criticized the GOP establishment on the low ranking in education funding.

"We learned a lot on this journey," he said. "We still broke a lot of records in Tennessee. We met a lot of people. We had the most money ever spent against an independent, that's a record, and we had the most votes for an independent ever."

No Democrat has won a statewide race in Tennessee since 2008 and Green came closer than any Democratic candidate since then in winning the governor's seat.

Early returns showed Blackburn ahead of Green, but Green pulled ahead several times as returns from Democratic strongholds of Memphis and Nashville came in — moments that ignited electric energy from her supporters in Chattanooga.

"It's been a very long time since there's been a governor race this close in this state," said former Tennessee Democratic Party Chair Hendrell Remus. "It's been a very long time since the governor's race hadn't been called this late on election night in a long time."

Remus thanked Green for "giving us something that no election result can ever take away: hope."

Green won Hamilton County, and easily surpassed the total statewide vote count won by former Nashville Mayor Karl Dean the last time Tennesseans elected a first-term governor in 2018. Surging independent candidate David Hatley lagged well behind both Blackburn and Green, but drew support from Blackburn.

"For years they told us that Tennessee wasn't worth the investment, that we're too red, that we're too much. It's too much hard work. That we don't vote enough. That there's not enough Democrats for that," Tennessee Democratic Party Chair Rachel Campbell told the crowd.

"Every Democrat who wins in Tennessee tonight will have been bolstered by her efforts," Campbell said of Green.

Inside the Blackburn and Green campaigns for Tennessee governor

Blackburn has made social issues like "transgender ideology" and opposition to communism central to her campaign. Her first TV ad showed her crushing fortune cookies and pledging to "crack down on China." Late in the race, she held a "Hold the Line" rally with retired Boston Celtics center Enes Kanter Freedom, who says he publicly identifies as a woman and declared himself eligible for the 2027 WNBA draft. Days before the election, Blackburn pledged on social media to "protect Tennessee from Sharia law and the spread of Islamization."

Following the failed execution attempt of Christa Pike, Blackburn said the state should bring back the electric chair. She pitched a "bell to bell, no cell" policy in public schools, and proposed a "Tennessee DOGE" to reduce state government bureaucracy , but did not identify what state departments or programs she would eliminate.

Despite long odds at the offset, Green crisscrossed the state meeting with voters and activating a Democratic base energized by a closer-than-ever special election in U.S. House District 7 and dissatisfaction with Republican incumbents. She held more than 210 public campaign stops.

Vivian Jones covers state government and politics for The Tennessean. Reach her at vjones@tennessean.com .

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, set to become 1st Muslim U.S. senator
articles.summary: His victory came after a bitter campaign that ended with his Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, endorsing his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
articles.body:
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won one of the marquee battles of the 2026 midterms : the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters in Michigan.

El-Sayed , an unapologetic 42-year-old progressive and the son of Egyptian immigrants, will become America's first Muslim senator. He has pushed policies such as Medicare for All and ending U.S. military aid to Israel, and has been willing to confront his critics and his own party's establishment.

His victory over Republican candidate Mike Rogers came on a night that saw Democrats regain control of the U.S. Senate in a midterm blue wave that also saw the party win control of the House of Representatives.

"You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates," El-Sayed told a crowd of supporters in Detroit on Wednesday as he declared victory. "Thank you. This is all yours."

El-Sayed defeated Rogers, a 63-year-old former congressman who lost an extremely close Senate race to Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin two years ago, and who has since broken with President Trump on tariffs and the war in Iran.

The race was rocked by several controversies, with the biggest coming two days before the election. Rep. Haley Stevens, the Democrat El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the primary, endorsed Rogers after she worshipped with the GOP candidate at Perfecting Church in Detroit.

"Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."

Stevens had said days earlier that she would vote for El-Sayed, and the two were due to appear together Sunday for the first time since August. That plan collapsed after she called on him to condemn an outside group's ad tying U.S. support for Israel to grocery prices. His campaign then asked her to stay away, NBC News reported . El-Sayed has stated he did not agree with the contents of the ad.

Defending her stance, Stevens told CNN on Sunday the decision was a "weight off my shoulders" and said she had decided to switch allegiances because El-Sayed had been getting "angrier and angrier" throughout the campaign.

When Stevens announced her change in support for Rogers, she maintained that she was "still a very proud Democrat." Michigan's Democratic Party chair, Curtis Hertel, fumed over the decision in a Sunday post on X , writing, "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."

Trump told a rally in Iowa on Sunday that he'd "love" Stevens to join the Republican Party and said she'd been "very brave" to endorse Rogers.

Rep. Debbie Dingell, who helped arrange the event, told the AP before the endorsement that she had called it off. "I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," she said.

"I would rather not distract from the key issues of this campaign," El-Sayed said Saturday . He attended a different Detroit church Sunday with Dingell and other Democrats, and did not address the dispute there, the AP reported.

On Sunday, El-Sayed spoke with reporters before a unity event with other Democrats and reacted to Stevens's endorsement, saying, "At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens."

"This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government. I'm a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about," El-Sayed said, referring to Stevens and Rogers.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on social media on Sunday that Stevens's reversal was a "despicable betrayal."

El-Sayed's background has made him the target of persistent attacks from Republicans, with Trump going so far as to call him a "jihadist" and accuse him of being "on the side of the terrorists."

Vice President JD Vance recently said El-Sayed had "zero attachment" to the United States. El-Sayed is a U.S. citizen who was born and raised in Michigan. Rogers has claimed, without evidence , that El-Sayed has supported the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

In a recent exchange at a town hall with a critic who asked him whether he denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed highlighted what he called the "implicit" suggestion in the question: the assumption that he'll have "dual loyalties" because of his faith.

"I'm not running to be a Muslim senator," he said. "I'm running for the U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim."

After Trump referred to El-Sayed as " Mohammed " — his middle name — the Democrat responded in what has become his signature pugnacious style.

"I don't care how he pronounces my name," El-Sayed said during a rally in Grand Rapids on Oct. 25. "Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."

Meanwhile, El-Sayed has campaigned with Hasan Piker , a Marxist streamer whom other Democrats have called antisemitic and even anti-American .

"If perfectly inoffensive won elections, then Donald Trump would never have been president," El-Sayed said in April when reporters questioned his choice of allies.

An independent left-wing group affiliated with Piker's uncle, commentator Cenk Uygur, also recently released an ad linking U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. The ad shows two parents shopping for their kids' lunch items; the mom tells the dad to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf.

"They don't like eggs anymore?" the dad asks.

"No, they like eggs," the mom answers. "But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians."

Some Democrats and Republicans have urged El-Sayed to denounce the content of the ad rather than just distancing himself from it.

"That has nothing to do with our campaign," El-Sayed said of the ad. "It's certainly not what I want to be talking about right now."

El-Sayed, 42, was born on Halloween 1984 in Rochester Hills, Mich. — a northern suburb of Detroit. His parents were immigrants from Egypt, and his first language was Arabic. He captained his high school's wrestling, football and lacrosse teams, then continued to play club lacrosse at the University of Michigan, where he majored in biology and political science.

El-Sayed went on to study medicine at Michigan, Oxford University (as a Rhodes Scholar) and Columbia University, where he received his MD. Before politics, he pursued a career in public health epidemiology as a tenure-track professor, and later led the Detroit health department.

In 2017, El-Sayed, then just 32, resigned as Detroit's health director to run for governor. He said at the time he was inspired by his work on the Flint water crisis . He was endorsed by prominent progressives — Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer by more than 20 percentage points.

After a stint as Wayne County health director, El-Sayed decided to try again in 2026. He has since become the most prominent Democratic insurgent to channel left-wing disillusionment with politics and outrage over Israel's actions in Gaza to win his party's nomination in a state where more moderate candidates typically prevail.

His argument is that even in so-called purple states such as Michigan, Democrats have a better shot at success when they pick buzzy, big-swing progressives over safe, "electable" incrementalists.

articles.title: Trump: ‘No plans’ to change Cabinet after GOP midterm losses
articles.summary: President Trump said he has no plans to change up his Cabinet after Democrats took control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. Trump, speaking with Fox News late Tuesday night, was asked whether he would make changes to his Cabinet considering the election results. “No, I don’t think so. Had nothing to…
articles.body:
President Trump said he has no plans to change up his Cabinet after Democrats took control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections .

Trump, speaking with Fox News late Tuesday night, was asked whether he would make changes to his Cabinet considering the election results.

“No, I don’t think so. Had nothing to do with my Cabinet,” Trump said.

“It was just a point — honestly, look — I’ve been doing a lot of great things for a long time,” he said. “It’s just a point in time. Just a point in time. Just the way it is. There was a mood in the air, I guess.”

Trump has ousted and seen some departures from his Cabinet this year, including the firing of both former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

CBS News reported some Trump aides are predicting that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could be a target of some of Trump’s blame for the party’s loss.

Trump told The Wall Street Journal that the Iran war “was a piece of” the cause of Republicans losing.

Democrats won control of the House and Senate Tuesday night, grabbing hold of some key races like the Texas, South Carolina and Kansas Senate seats, among others.

Trump said the loss was due to him not being on the ballot and repeatedly said that the president’s party usually doesn’t win the midterms.

“I shouldn’t feel guilty because virtually … no matter how good or bad or Republican or Democrat he or she is, but no matter how good the president is, you lose,” Trump said.

“I don’t know why. Nobody’s explained that, but it’s almost every single time,” he continued.

Trump told the outlet that voters just “didn’t like the candidates.”

Earlier Tuesday, Trump said Republicans lost because he wasn’t on the ballot.

“And if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he wrote on Truth Social. “Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

articles.title: Democrat unseats Barrett in battleground Michigan House contest
articles.summary: Democrats are projected to score a big win in Michigan, with William Lawrence, a liberal climate activist, picking off GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in the state’s 7th District, according to Decision Desk HQ. Heading into the polls, the race was a true toss-up, with both sides spending enormously to make it one of the most…
articles.body:
Democrats are projected to score a big win in Michigan, with William Lawrence, a liberal climate activist, picking off GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in the state’s 7th District, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Heading into the polls, the race was a true toss-up, with both sides spending enormously to make it one of the most expensive contests of the 2026 cycle. Lawrence garnered about 51 percent of the vote while the incumbent notched about 48 percent, with more than 95 percent of the vote tallied Wednesday morning.

Republicans were confident that Barrett, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, would hold the seat that includes the state’s capital of Lansing, especially given Lawrence’s prior affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). GOP operatives sought to highlight that history, arguing that Lawrence — who had defeated two centrist Democrats in the primary in August — was simply too far left for the purple 7th District.

It wasn’t enough to save Barrett, however, in a cycle when President Trump’s historic unpopularity, the Iran war and widespread economic anxieties have been a drag on GOP candidates across the country.

Lawrence played to those anxieties, focusing his campaign message on the kitchen-table issue of affordability, including efforts to shore up Social Security, bring down the cost of housing and establish a system of universal healthcare.

He also vowed to end the conflict in Iran and install a yearlong, national moratorium on the construction of new data centers — an issue that has resonated around the country in the lead-up to the elections.

Lawrence is a political newcomer but no stranger to Washington politics. He’s a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, which was established to push policymakers at all levels to get tougher on climate change.

The group made waves in 2018 when it led a protest at the Washington office of then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) — a sit-in attended by the newly elected Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.).

Lawrence left the DSA just weeks before his primary victory this year. But his ties to the group and activist history will make him among the most closely watched new Democrats in the Capitol, where Democratic leaders will face the daunting challenge of balancing the interests of rabble-rousing progressives with those of the centrists.

articles.title: Democrat Christina Hines flips House seat in Michigan
articles.summary: Democratic prosecutor Christina Hines was projected to defeat Republican Army veteran Mike Bouchard in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), flipping a GOP-held seat in the suburbs of Detroit. Hines will succeed Rep. John James (R-Mich.), who ran for governor this year with President Trump’s endorsement instead of seeking a third…
articles.body:
Democratic prosecutor Christina Hines was projected to defeat Republican Army veteran Mike Bouchard in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District , according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), flipping a GOP-held seat in the suburbs of Detroit.

Hines will succeed Rep. John James (R-Mich.), who ran for governor this year with President Trump’s endorsement instead of seeking a third term. The district covers much of southern Macomb County and part of Oakland County.

The open seat was a top target for Democrats.

The district voted for Trump three times over his opponents: by 5 points in 2016, by 1 point in 2020 and by nearly 7 points in 2024. But it also backed Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D) by double digits in 2022 — when James narrowly won his first term. Benson was on the ballot again this year, also running for governor .

James’s departure gave Democrats an opening by removing Republicans’ incumbency advantage. In August, Cook Political Report moved the race from “lean Republican” to toss-up. As of Monday, DDHQ rated the race as “lean Democrat,” giving Hines a 66 percent chance of winning.

Hines won a competitive Democratic primary this year by 17 points despite being outraised by two opponents. Cook Political Report attributes her success, in part, to her strong support in Macomb County.

A former prosecutor in Wayne and Washtenaw counties, Hines focused her campaign on lowering costs, expanding access to affordable healthcare and fighting corruption, including by banning members of Congress from trading stocks . She also sought to tie her opponent to Trump, who endorsed Bouchard.

The GOP hopeful, a former Army paratrooper, is the son of longtime Oakland County Sheriff Michael Bouchard, who won reelection in 2024 by more than 20 points. The Republican focused his campaign on supporting domestic manufacturing and auto jobs in the district, securing the southern border and addressing inflation.

articles.title: GOP’s Moore, Knott, McDowell ousted in North Carolina House races
articles.summary: The Democrats in three North Carolina districts are on track to oust their incumbent Republican opponents in their respective neck-and-neck House races. In the race for North Carolina’s 13th Congressional District, Democrat Paul Barringer is projected to defeat incumbent Republican Rep. Brad Knott, according to preliminary results from election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). The…
articles.body:
The Democrats in three North Carolina districts are on track to oust their incumbent Republican opponents in their respective neck-and-neck House races.

In the race for North Carolina’s 13th Congressional District, Democrat Paul Barringer is projected to defeat incumbent Republican Rep. Brad Knott, according to preliminary results from election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

The Democrat won with more than 50 percent support while the incumbent garnered a little more than 48 percent, with more than 95 percent of votes tallied.

Democratic candidate Lakesha Womack is projected to win against Republican Rep. Tim Moore in the state’s 14th Congressional District, DDHQ’s projection shows.

Womack won with more than 51 percent support while Moore received nearly 49 percent, with 95 percent of votes tallied.

In the state’s 6th Congressional District, Democrat Cyril Jefferson is projected to oust incumbent Republican Rep. Addison McDowell, DDHQ projects .

Jefferson earned more than 51 percent support to the Republican’s nearly 49 percent, with 95 percent of the votes tallied.

In the state’s competitive Senate race to fill the seat vacated by Sen. Thom Tillis (R), former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D) defeated former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, flipping the Senate seat blue .

The Democratic wins in the Tar Heel State are consistent with the overall midterm results across the country, where the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and the House in a sweeping victory .

articles.title: The House Committee on Agriculture has advanced forestry. Congress must finish the job
articles.summary: House Agriculture Committee Chairman Glenn GT Thompson and Forest Landowners Association CEO Scott Jones are urging Congress to pass legislation, including a new farm bill and the Save America’s Family Forests Act, to support timber landowners struggling with disaster recovery and market instability.
articles.body:
A family forest landowner can spend 30 years growing a stand of timber and lose it to a hurricane in an afternoon.

Hurricane Helene, a category four storm that made landfall in September of 2024, caused an estimated $1.28 billion in timber damage across Georgia alone. Nearly 9 million acres of forestland were impacted by Helene, and 88 percent of impacted forestland was privately owned.

For those families, the losses represent generations of investment, and recovering these forests is expensive.

America’s working forests support rural jobs, wildlife habitat, clean water, recreation, and a domestic supply of renewable wood products. Keeping them productive requires disaster recovery tools and a return on the timber landowners grow. The House Committee on Agriculture has made meaningful progress on these challenges — Congress must now build on that work to keep America’s working forests successful for generations to come.

This year, the House of Representatives passed the Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026 , also known as the farm bill, which contains a strong forestry title to address the many issues before our national forests and non-federal forestlands. The House-passed farm bill provides reforms to improve management, partnerships, the forest products industry, and forest health. Now that the Senate Agriculture Committee has begun the process in the upper chamber by advancing its version of the farm bill, it is time for Congress to come together and deliver a final bill before the end of the year.

The House Committee on Agriculture’s work also helped deliver a bipartisan law addressing an immediate challenge: paying for recovery before assistance arrives. The Emergency Conservation Program Improvement Act became law this year. It allows eligible nonindustrial private forest landowners to receive advance payments for qualifying emergency restoration measures, helping them begin recovery without shouldering all eligible costs upfront.

These advances matter. But restoring a working forest also requires access to strong timber markets and the financial ability to replant. Emergency assistance alone cannot solve the loss of a nearby mill or the cost of starting another decades-long growing cycle.

Timber markets face pressure as mills close, demand changes, and outlets for lower-value wood products shrink. The consequences extend beyond the mill gate. Landowners lose markets, loggers lose work and truckers lose loads. These continued losses weaken our rural communities, contributing to further population flight to suburbs and cities.

Without a viable return from timber, landowners face hard decisions about whether they can afford to keep their land in forestry. Strong markets help sustain forest ownership and management.

Forest policy must support markets that make active management and recovery economically viable.

The bipartisan Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act will help accomplish that by modernizing the Renewable Fuel Standard’s definition of renewable biomass to include more of the low-value woody material generated through forest management, hazardous-fuels reduction, ecological restoration and forest products manufacturing.

New markets for material removed to reduce wildfire risk can offset management costs, reduce hazardous fuels and turn a disposal problem into an opportunity for American forest products and renewable energy.

Landowners also need modern tools to replant after disaster.

Under current law, timberland owners can deduct up to $10,000 annually in qualified reforestation expenses per qualified timber property, with additional costs amortized over seven years. That limit dates to 2004. Site preparation, seedlings and planting now cost substantially more, and catastrophic storms like Hurricane Helene can leave landowners facing expenses far beyond that limit.

The bipartisan Save America’s Family Forests Act will raise the annual reforestation deduction from $10,000 to $30,000 and allow an immediate deduction of up to $500,000 in qualifying reforestation expenses following federally declared natural disasters.

Updating this existing tax provision would help landowners reinvest sooner, recognizing that the cost of establishing a forest comes decades before the income from harvesting it.

The House Committee on Agriculture has helped lay the foundation for a more resilient timber economy and more responsible stewardship of our natural resources. Completing the job requires cooperation across Congress, including the committees responsible for energy policy and the tax code. Landowners experience disaster recovery, timber markets and reforestation as connected challenges. Congress must address them accordingly.

Congress should reauthorize a new farm bill and advance the bipartisan Save America’s Family Forests Act and Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act. An end-of-year legislative package offers an opportunity to build on this progress and give landowners the tools to remain productive, rather than forcing the country to watch a critical industry struggle for lack of governmental support.

The job is not finished. Healthy, resilient forests for the next generation depend on landowners being able to recover from disasters, find markets for their timber and afford to plant again.

That is how we keep America’s working forests working.

Glenn “GT” Thompson represents Pennsylvania’s 15th District and chairs the House Committee on Agriculture. Scott Jones is CEO of the Forest Landowners Association.

articles.title: Democratic socialist wins DC mayor’s office
articles.summary: Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George was projected to win the race for mayor of Washington and lead the nation’s capital through the end of President Trump’s second term, according to Decision Desk HQ. Retiring Mayor Muriel Bowser (D) has led the city for a decade, tangling with the Trump administration over crime, public safety and…
articles.body:
Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George was projected to win the race for mayor of Washington and lead the nation’s capital through the end of President Trump’s second term, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Retiring Mayor Muriel Bowser (D) has led the city for a decade, tangling with the Trump administration over crime, public safety and the president’s changes to the District . Lewis George garnered about 86 percent of the vote, per DDHQ.

Lewis George emerged this summer from a crowded Democratic primary, the first in two decades without an incumbent on the ballot. She defeated a more moderate competitor as progressives notched key midterm wins across the country.

Roughly three-quarters of D.C. voters are registered Democrats , leading to friction between the city’s leaders and the Republicans controlling the White House and Capitol Hill.

Trump last year took federal control of the D.C. police department and deployed the National Guard in the city, claiming that the capital had been “overtaken by violent gangs and bloodthirsty criminals, roving mobs of wild youth, drugged-out maniacs and homeless people.”

Crime was down 35 percent in D.C. in 2024, marking a 30-year low. It dropped 18 percent in 2025, the first year of Trump’s second term, according to data from the District.

Lewis George, a former prosecutor who has served on the D.C. Council for six years, pledged to “work with anyone to the benefit of D.C. residents,” calling work with the federal government “an essential” in an interview with 7News just ahead of Election Day.

Lewis George joins New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as another member of the Democratic Socialists of America to win the mayor’s office in a major blue city.

Amid the primary, Trump warned that the government could “take back” D.C. if a “crazy socialist” was ultimately elected.

articles.summary: Republican Jon Bonck is projected to win the open Texas House race to replace outgoing Rep. Wesley Hunt (R), according to Decision Desk HQ. The GOP candidate defeated Democratic opponent Melissa McDonough in the race to represent the state’s 38th District. He notched just more than 51 percent of the vote to McDonough’s 47 percent, as…
articles.body:
Republican Jon Bonck is projected to win the open Texas House race to replace outgoing Rep. Wesley Hunt (R), according to Decision Desk HQ.

The GOP candidate defeated Democratic opponent Melissa McDonough in the race to represent the state’s 38th District. He notched just more than 51 percent of the vote to McDonough’s 47 percent, as of Wednesday afternoon.

Bonck, who handily won the GOP primary in May, ran on strengthening border security , protecting Second Amendment rights, cutting spending for foreign wars and supporting President Trump’s agenda.

Trump backed Bonck’s campaign in a Truth Social post ahead of the Republican primary, granting the mortgage banker and real estate small business owner his “Complete and Total Endorsement” in this race.

“A successful Business Executive, Jon knows the America First Policies required to Create GREAT Jobs, Cut Taxes and Regulations, Promote MADE IN THE U.S.A., Unleash American Energy DOMINANCE, and Champion our Nation’s Golden Age,” Trump wrote.

“In Congress, he will fight tirelessly to Keep our Border SECURE, Stop Migrant Crime, Strengthen our Military/Veterans, Safeguard our Elections, and Protect our always under siege Second Amendment,” he continued.

The 38th District is in the southeastern region of the state and includes parts of the Houston suburbs. Hunt has represented the district since 2023, before he left to launch an unsuccessful Senate bid.

articles.title: It’s too close to call in these Senate, House races
articles.summary: Plus: 🏠Johnson triggers leadership fight {beacon} It’s Wednesday. We tried to sleep, briefly. Wow, did Election Day fly by. In today’s issue: The blue wave hits hard Awaiting Mississippi, Alaska results Undecided House races Johnson won’t run for minority leader Trump, Vance react to drubbing First College Football Playoff rankings Programming note: We’re Joshua Feldstein and Julia…
articles.body:
It’s Wednesday. We tried to sleep, briefly. Wow, did Election Day fly by.

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Julia Boehning, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and jboehning@thehill.com.

⚖️ The legal battles aren’t taking a break after Election Day! The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams unpack the fight over Trump’s D.C. arch project, Mississippi’s nail-biting Senate race and more on “The Gavel.” Insiders to join the live discussion at 3 p.m. EST.

Sarah Warnock and Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press

After a wild Tuesday night, two key Senate races head into Wednesday afternoon still awaiting final results — with one being more of a surprise than the other.

The Mississippi Senate race has shockingly come down to the wire, with Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith neck-and-neck.

As of 12:27 p.m., Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, reported that over 95 percent of the vote has been counted. With nearly all of the votes counted on Wednesday morning, Colom led Hyde-Smith by a little over 1,300 votes.

Seven and counting: If Colom wins, it would be the eighth Senate seat to flip for Democrats. President Trump notably won Mississippi by 20 percentage points in 2024.

In the days leading up to Election Day, all eyes were on the Alaska Senate race between former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan .

Accusations came out last week that Peltola’s campaign was directly involved in getting a “decoy” candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr ., to join the state race. She denied the accusations and said she was “so deeply offended” by the reports.

A Department of Justice (DOJ) lawsuit to block the certification of the election was tossed out, but could be revived when results are final.

As of Wednesday morning, Peltola holds 48.2 percent of the vote compared to Sullivan’s 47.9 percent. DDHQ is reporting about 69 percent of the vote has been counted.

Sullivan Jr., an independent, has secured 1.7 percent of the state’s vote, or some 3,500 votes.

How long could it take for a decision?: Alaska officials have said it could take up to two weeks before the Peltola vs. Sullivan race is decided, since neither appears to be on track to win a majority in the first round of ranked-choice voting.

Many House races stretching from Maine to California are still up in the air as of Wednesday morning, with some being separated by only a few hundred votes.

Pine Tree anxiety: Maine’s 2nd Congressional District between Republican Paul LePage , the former governor, and Democrat Matt Dunlap , the state’s auditor, are split by fewer than 1,000 votes as of Wednesday morning, according to DDHQ.

The seat was vacated by retiring Rep. Jared Golden (D), who has often split from the Democratic Party.

Heating up in Arizona: The 8th Congressional District is coming down to the wire for Republican incumbent Abraham Hamadeh , who only leads Democratic challenger Bernadette Greene-Placentia by a few thousand votes.

As of Wednesday morning, Hamadeh led Greene-Placentia 51.1 percent to 48.9 percent, according to DDHQ projections.

Arizona’s 2nd Congressional District is also growing increasingly tight for Republican incumbent Eli Crane , who is locked in an extremely tight matchup with Democrat Jonathan Nez .

As of 10:10 a.m. EST, Nez led Crane by only 86 votes with a little over 79 percent of the vote accounted for, according to DDHQ.

Rocky (who’s on) top: Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District could also see a Republican House seat flip, with Democrat Victoria Broderick holding on to a 280-vote lead over Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R) as of Wednesday morning.

DesJarlais had a 97 percent chance to secure the Tennessee House seat ahead of the midterm election, per DDHQ projections, but Broderick can now flip a ruby red district.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Wednesday he would not launch a bid to continue leading the House GOP in the minority, two staffers with the party told The Hill.

Now that Johnson’s out of the running, contenders for minority leader role including House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) — a potentially dicey face-off as Republicans readjust to a predominately blue lower chamber.

Though recent House Speakers have stepped out of Congress after losing the gavel, Johnson last week hinted at plans to buck the trend. The shakeup comes as Republicans near their congressional leadership elections, which are set for Nov. 10.

🔎 The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi has more on this developing story here .

As the blue wave came into focus, the White House quickly pointed blame at the Republican candidates, despite Trump’s midterm blitz urging voters to pretend he was on the ballot.

“President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot,” a White House official said.

Trump blamed the losses on Fox News in angry posts on Truth Social, and again while appearing on the network after midnight.

He did acknowledge that his war in Iran “was a piece of” Republicans’ poor performance.

In Texas, he blamed Gov. Greg Abbott (R) for his stunning loss to Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Vance speaks: Vice President Vance went further than Trump, squarely blaming the Iran war for the disastrous election results.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a post on X . “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

Mr. Veto? The president sent mixed messages surrounding his future dynamic with Democrat-controlled Congress. Though he told several news outlets in late-night call-ins to news outlets he was willing to work with the left for the latter half of his final term, he also posted an image to Truth Social of a MAGA-like hat with the word “veto.”

🔎 Read a full report by The Hill’s Dominick Mastrangelo on Trump’s election night Fox frustration here .

🗳️ Iran’s top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf weighed in on the U.S.’s midterm results, saying, “Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”

🌵 In one of the first major races to be announced on Wednesday , Nevada Democrat Aaron Ford has flipped the state’s governor’s mansion, defeating Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo , DDHQ reports.

🐸 The Trump administration has moved to drop charges against a Harvard University researcher who was accused of smuggling frog embryos into the U.S. Kseniia Petrova , a Russian-born scientist, has her visa canceled by the administration and looked to deport her, but in the latest development, the government said it is dropping its charges.

🤝 Ohio Governor-elect Amy Acton (D) paused her victory speech on Tuesday night to help someone in the crowd who reportedly passed out.

🔄 Democrat Richard Ojeda flipped North Carolina’s 8th Congressional District in a major upset on Wednesday morning over incumbent Rep. Richard Hudson (R), who led the House Republican campaign arm this cycle.

Politico: Tehran gloats as Republicans take a beating

The New York Times: How Americans Voted in 2026

NBC News: 5 key insights from the NBC News Exit Poll about the blue tsunami

The Washington Post: D.C. elected its first democratic socialist mayor. What does it mean for the city?

The House and Senate are out. President Trump is in Washington but has no public events on his schedule.

🍬 Celebrate : Today is National Candy Day! Enjoy some of your favorite sweets while watching The Hill break down yesterday’s craziness (also so close to Halloween?).

🏈The first College Football Playoff bracket was released on Tuesday night, ranking the Miami Hurricanes, Georgia Bulldogs, Utah Utes and Indiana Hoosiers as the top four seeds.

Were you up all night keeping track of election results? Us, too! Give your brain a break and spend 30 seconds just watching these adorable lion cubs 🦁

We love hearing from you — send your feedback, tips and favorite cookie recipes 🍪 to jfeldstein@thehill.com and jboehning@thehill.com .

Check out more newsletters here . See you next time!

articles.title: DeSantis on GOP pummeling: ‘Close to an extinction-level event for Republicans’
articles.summary: Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) called the wave of GOP losses in Tuesday’s midterm election “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans.” “This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country, as we have seen probably in the last 100 years,” he said during a Wednesday press conference.…
articles.body:
Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) called the wave of GOP losses in Tuesday’s midterm election “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans.”

“This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country, as we have seen probably in the last 100 years, ” he said during a Wednesday press conference .

“In January, when everyone in office leaves who are either term-limited or got voted out, of the 10 largest states in this union, only one state will have Republican control … the state of Florida.”

Republicans narrowly hung on to Florida on Election Day, retaining seats in the Senate and the governor’s mansion by close margins, though Democrats still won some redistricted House seats meant to favor GOP candidates.

“Let’s just be clear that that is going to hurt. Not just for the next two years, that’s something that can reverberate for the next decade or more,” DeSantis said.

He then pointed to his party’s historic losses in Texas, which he called the “crown jewel of Republican politics,” both up and down ballot. He noted that without the Lone Star State, the GOP is “not going to be viable nationally going forward.”

Last night, Democrat James Talarico became the first member of his party to win a Texas Senate seat in decades, defeating state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). Incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) also took a stunning loss to Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa.

Democrats also won big in other Republican strongholds like Iowa and Kansas.

“We knew it could be worse, but I don’t think most of us thought it would be quite this bad,” the outgoing Florida governor added. “This was a rejection of Republicans in Washington, and Democrats just happened to be the beneficiary. Now it’s going to take a lot of time and effort to rebuild.”

In a lengthy Wednesday morning post to the social platform X, Vice President Vance cited four reasons voters chose to not vote for the GOP: the war in Iran, living costs, not putting “America First” and the U.S.’s relationship with Israel.

“Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats,” Vance wrote.

articles.title: Schumer has votes for majority leader despite some Democratic dissent
articles.summary: Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) says he will be reelected as Senate majority leader next month when Democrats hold leadership elections despite the dissent of a handful of newly elected senators who threatened not to support him serving another term as leader. “The issue is not me. I’ll be reelected as majority leader. But the issue…
articles.body:
Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) says he will be reelected as Senate majority leader next month when Democrats hold leadership elections despite the dissent of a handful of newly elected senators who threatened not to support him serving another term as leader.

“The issue is not me. I’ll be reelected as majority leader. But the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want,” Schumer told reporters when asked about victorious candidates who said they would not vote for him as leader, including Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Troy Jackson in Maine and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

Schumer needs only a majority of the Democratic caucus, which is projected to have at least 54 members and possibly as many as 56 in 2027.

Other Democrats who have threatened not to back Schumer for leader include Juliana Stratton, who won Illinois’s Senate seat, and Peggy Flanagan, who won Minnesota’s Senate seat.

Beyond that, Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for a “new generation” of leaders in the party.

While some Democrats have said they want new leadership in the Senate or have called more vaguely for generational change, it appears Schumer will remain firmly in control of the Senate Democratic caucus with broad support after Democrats had a huge night on Tuesday.

Schumer played a key role in recruiting successful candidates in key races, such as former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in North Carolina, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) in Ohio and potentially former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) in Alaska.

Schumer, however, has been sure to give credit to his Senate Democratic colleagues for Tuesday’s pickup of at least seven Republican-held seats across the country.

“We spent a year and a half in the Senate as a Democratic caucus — I got to thank my caucus members. They were amazing as well, not only in finding unity in these issues, but in, you know, if you looked at a map a week before the election, you probably have three-quarters of the caucus in different states campaigning with our candidates,” he said during an interview with MS NOW’s “Morning Joe.”

Asked about criticism of his leadership from frustrated Democrats in recent years, Schumer responded, “This is not about me.”

“This is about the American people and what they want and what they need and what we can do to help them. Plain and simple,” he said Wednesday at a press conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters.

articles.title: Oklahoma City’s GOP mayor: ‘Morally and intellectually bankrupt’ party deserved ‘rebuke’
articles.summary: Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt (R) criticized his own party Tuesday, saying the GOP deserved the “rebuke” of the American people amid the Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the midterm elections. “A political party that is morally and intellectually bankrupt deserves the rebuke of the American people,” Holt wrote on social media Tuesday night. “It…
articles.body:
Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt (R) criticized his own party Tuesday, saying the GOP deserved the “rebuke” of the American people amid the Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the midterm elections.

“A political party that is morally and intellectually bankrupt deserves the rebuke of the American people,” Holt wrote on social media Tuesday night. “It is now time to make America good again.”

Democrats secured control of both the House and the Senate, including Senate wins in battleground states like Texas, Michigan, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa.

GOP candidates maintained a strong hold in Oklahoma, with Republican Rep. Kevin Hern defeating Democrat N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas in a competitive race for the state’s open Senate seat . However, in the neighboring states of Texas and Kansas, Democrats secured historic wins.

Texas Democratic candidates James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa defeated their Republican opponents, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, respectively, in the state’s Senate and gubernatorial races.

Talarico will be the first Democrat to hold a Senate seat in the Lone Star State since 1988.

In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall. Hamilton will be the first Democratic senator from the Sunflower State since 1939.

“We are humans, and the things that unite us far exceed the things that divide us. We are the caretakers of the American experiment, and the experiment has been rejuvenated tonight,” Holt said in his post.

articles.title: Pfluger challenges Emmer for minority whip position
articles.summary: Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (R-Texas) is running against House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) for the minority whip position after Democrats won control of the lower chamber. Pfluger wrote in a letter to his Republican colleagues on Wednesday the GOP must be “crafting a strategy to win back the majority.” “We started 2025…
articles.body:
Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (R-Texas) is running against House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) for the minority whip position after Democrats won control of the lower chamber.

Pfluger wrote in a letter to his Republican colleagues on Wednesday the GOP must be “crafting a strategy to win back the majority.”

“We started 2025 with a clear mandate, and although there were successes, I believe we left a lot on the table,” Pfluger wrote. “Some circumstances may have been out of our control, but we also missed many opportunities.”

Pfluger added that Republicans “need fresh ideas and a leadership team committed to rebuilding a culture with a clear game plan to win in 2028.”

“I’m running for Republican Whip because I believe that I am capable and can be trusted to implement the changes this team needs,” Pfluger added. “From day one in Congress, I have devoted myself towards helping others and that is exactly what I will continue to do in this role.”

Emmer previously said in an interview with Axios that he plans on being in the whip position rather than running for another leadership post.

“I love my job. I would love to continue being the whip. If they want to hire somebody else, that’ll be up to the members. But I’m going to continue doing this job as long as they give me the privilege of doing this job,” Emmer told Axios in September.

His tenure as majority whip has been marked by deep divisions within the conference, with conservative hard-liners at times blocking legislation from advancing on the House floor.

“As your Republican Whip, I will continue to be direct, honest, and transparent,” Emmer said in a dear colleague letter to Republicans on Wednesday.

“We have never made false promises or tried to buy your votes. My role is to support every Member of this conference and help you succeed. Success will feel different in the minority – and often less satisfying – but will require no less support and unity in our conference.”

Emmer also touted his achievements as the previous chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

“It has always been my top priority to help our House Republican team succeed. Over the last eight years, I have dedicated myself to growing and supporting this group. Wehn I took over the NRCC in 2019, we needed to change. We needed to install a winning culture. In 2020, we were expected to lose up to 24 seats,” Emmer said.

“We fought tooth and nail, and gained a historic 15 seats, nearly flipping the House in a presidential year. In 2022, we finished the job. We’ve taken on the tough fights as a team, and won. We must return to that same mindset to retake the majority in two years.”

articles.title: Amid the Trump wreckage, the free press survives
articles.summary: The American free press will survive now and for decades to come.
articles.body:
If having presidents make life difficult for the news media could destroy First Amendment protections, the free press would have ceased operation countless times over the course of American history.

Pretty much every president has battled the press, including founding fathers John Adams and Thomas Jefferson. Abraham Lincoln saved the union, but was ruthless in stifling journalists and editors . Woodrow Wilson treated the press just as badly . Harry Truman’s “give ‘em hell” approach certainly applied to the press, calling reporters “prostitutes of the mind.” Barack Obama surveilled a number of journalists , including reporters from the AP, The New York Times, CBS and FNC.

Despite many challenges, the free press has survived. The press has continued to abide by its constitutional functions, just as the framers intended. The American free press will survive now and for decades to come.

Today’s press acts as a watchdog as intended, hassling the current occupant of the White House, who in turn is carrying on the presidential tradition of barking back at the watchdog. But to hear the persistent shrill cries and howls of journalists , you’d think Donald Trump had taken a wrecking ball to the First Amendment.

Trump does certainly loathe the establishment press, and seldom misses an opportunity to scold and berate journalists. He recently insulted a Reuters reporter about his physical condition after the reporter asked about the president’s travel schedule. And he has sought to restrict politically unfriendly media outlets such as CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House press facilities.

Trump also likes to sue the press for defamation, surely knowing his suits have virtually no chance of success. A federal judge just tossed Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal for publishing a story about a birthday card he allegedly sent to Jeffrey Epstein more than two decades ago. Trump did win some measly settlements from ABC and CBS , but that’s just because those outlets wimped out.

No doubt, the news industry feels bruised and battered by such hostile treatment from the White House. The issue, however, is not whether Trump’s antagonism hurts journalists’ feelings with his admittedly unpolished behavior. It is whether Trump is doing genuine harm to the First Amendment.

If Trump has wrecked the First Amendment, one must wonder how so much anti-Trump reportage continues to appear.

At last check, all of the media outlets Trump loves to hate were still committing journalism, publishing and broadcasting as they like. The president’s antagonism and bullying has not intimidated the likes of CNN or The New York Times, as those outlets and others fearlessly bash the president with as much negative reporting as they can muster. The free press climate doesn’t appear to be chilled.

The press, of course, doesn’t like Trump’s caustic insults, but the president has his own free speech rights to rhetorically brawl with the media, even if it does seem unproductive. Reporters who want to sulk because Trump is mean to them should find alternative career paths.

The media industry has battled back in the legal arena as well, filing lawsuits to counter the White House barrage. The Knight First Amendment Institute and individual media outlets have suits pending that, if successful, would reverse Trump administration sanctions against various White House reporters.

What’s more, the White House has not crossed the line on the most important rights of a free press. The Freedom of Information Act is still intact. No reporters are in custody. Prior restraint, a key to First Amendment rights, has not been flexed to keep journalists from publishing whatever they want. Sure, the Trump White House is hostile to the news industry, but the American press is still free.

For a president who despises the press, Trump gives unprecedented opportunity for reporters to engage him. He has by far given more briefings and press gaggles than any president in history. If Trump were really trying to destroy press freedom, he certainly wouldn’t engage reporters so frequently.

Journalists just can’t expect the government to make life easy for them. Former Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart made that point clear in a seminal address to Yale Law School in 1974. Stewart said the press is free to battle the government, “But the press cannot expect from the Constitution any guarantee it will succeed.” He also said the press has no right to access the government bureaucracy. “The Constitution, in other words, establishes the contest, not its resolution.”

When it comes to press freedom, the United States is still the envy of the world. The biggest threat to press freedom today, however, is not from without — the White House, the courts or government bureaucracy. It is from within. Public confidence in press performance has sunk over the years.

Thomas Jefferson warned early in the nation’s history that the press was its own worst enemy. “It is a melancholy truth, that a suppression of the press could not more completely deprive the nation of its benefits, than is done by its abandoned prostitution to falsehood.”

The media industry will surely survive Trump. The bigger challenge is to survive its own failings.

Jeffrey M. McCall is a media critic and professor of communication at DePauw University. He has worked as a radio news director, a newspaper reporter and as a political media consultant.

articles.title: Republicans annihilated in midterms: Anti-war MAGA was right
articles.summary: When you break a promise, your voters punish you.
articles.body:
Well, the results are in, and the Republican Party got absolutely annihilated in the midterm elections. They massively lost the House, as expected, and they also lost the Senate, as I predicted. But Democrats won way, way, way more seats than even the most partisan leftists dreamed they would get.

Democrats won Texas by huge margins: James Talarico beat Ken Paxton. They won in South Carolina, where Lindsey Graham’s sister went down to defeat. They won in quintessential red states like Kansas and Ohio and Iowa. It’s so bad the anticipated Fetterman flip won’t save the GOP. Nothing will. It’s so bad that Donald Trump had little choice but to accept how bad it was, pledging to accept the results, work with Democrats wherever possible, and veto bad legislation they might propose. As he should.

But policy comes later. Right now we need to understand what went wrong.

Two years ago, Trump won a massive victory over the Democratic coalition, bringing in new voters, minority voters, men, young people. He exposed the hollowness of the Kamala Harris campaign and achieved a mandate to cut government — which became the DOGE initiative — and to avoid foreign entanglements. No new wars! That was Trump’s promise.

And let me be clear: more than anything else, that broken promise, the Iran War, is clearly why Trump’s voters did not show up for him last night. It has been obvious for weeks, to anyone who was paying attention, that Americans are furious about high energy prices that are downstream of this reckless attack on Iran, that was never justified to the American people and never voted on by Congress, and that went entirely contrary to Trump’s campaign promise.

When you break a promise, your voters punish you. George H.W. Bush learned that with “read my lips, no new taxes.” Now Trump is learning it.

And the price is high. A moderate comeuppance for the GOP might have been well deserved to get them back on track, but this is perhaps the most staggering rebuke of the incumbent party in American politics in my lifetime. Only Barack Obama’s trifecta + 60 in the Senate in 2008 comes close. Thankfully, Democrats will not be in a position to pass legislation — Trump can veto it. But they will be in a position to launch investigations of the Trump family, the administration and Trump supporters, from the lowliest to the highest, including Elon Musk.

That will be the Democratic agenda. I would not rule out the possibility that they try to impeach Trump again, and make no mistake, they are very, very close to having the votes to pull that off.

That is the cost of this reckless war: The end of the Trump agenda, forever. Trump will never again have the kind of political power he had to enact the America First agenda.

Certainly the president himself deserves blame for this, and deep down he knows it. But we must also blame the neoconservative advisers who urged him to do something his voters did not want: initiate a costly conflict with a distant foreign nation that is largely irrelevant to our own security. They have desired this war forever, and Trump gave it to them. And it has destroyed his party.

Every hawkish GOP hack who said the war would be over quickly, or it wouldn’t matter for midterms, or the concerns were overblown, is a fool or a liar. On the other hand, every America First populist or libertarian who said, “hey wait a minute, why are we doing this,” was absolutely correct to sound the alarm. It was foolishness — no, it was madness. And now the chickens have come home to roost.

The Democrats didn’t just beat Republicans, they destroyed them. Their victories were so absolute that candidate quality didn’t matter. With the exception of Florida, the sole bright spot for the GOP, basically the story is that every single Republican who could lose did lose. All of them. Every single one. They lost in the Senate races, they lost in the House races, they lost in the state legislatures and governors’ races.

You can’t sugarcoat this: It’s a blowout that would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. Oh, by the way, a few months ago, the Iran War was in its infancy, and had not yet damaged the economy. Once voters understood Trump wasn’t ending it, they decided to punish him. And so they have.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

Editor’s note: This article has been updated to correct the location in which Sticker Mule is based.

Sticker company CEO Anthony Constantino (R) is projected to win Rep. Elise Stefanik’s (R-N.Y.) open House seat, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s partner.

Constantino, who was endorsed by President Trump, defeated Democrat Blake Gendebien and independent Christopher Schmidt in the race to represent the Empire State’s 21st District. Republicans were likely to win the seat, per DDHQ. The Republican notched just under 51 percent of the vote, with more than 95 percent of the vote tallied as of Wednesday afternoon.

While on the campaign trail, Constantino touted his record as a successful business owner of Sticker Mule. According to its website , the company is based in New York but also has manufacturing facilities in South Carolina and Italy.

Outside of his work, Constantino also noted his participation in boxing tournaments — winning his debut match in Coacalco, Mexico, a town just north of Mexico City.

He campaigned on eliminating government waste, lowering utility pricing, securing the country’s northern border and growing New York’s Republican Party, according to his campaign website .

Stefanik, who held the seat for six terms and is seen as rising star within the GOP, opted to not seek reelection and elected to instead run in New York’s gubernatorial race.

She dropped her gubernatorial bid last December in a stunning announcement from the lawmaker, who once rose in leadership to be the House’s No. 4 Republican .

articles.title: DeSantis: Republicans denying soaring costs are gaslighting voters
articles.summary: The midterm results are a reminder that elections have consequences, even for a president who says he doesn’t care about them.
articles.body:
On Election Night, Joe Scarborough pulled out a handwritten list of the controversies surrounding President Trump’s administration this year, from grifting accusations to the Epstein files to Operation Metro Surge, and questioned how Republicans managed to accumulate so many political liabilities in such a short period of time.

“You’ve got the Big Beautiful Bill, you’ve got the slashing of health care, you’ve got tariffs. I still believe that when history books are written, that Minneapolis will be the end. That will be the Pickett’s Charge version of this administration.”

For context, Pickett’s Charge was the disastrous Confederate assault at Gettysburg, a turning point in the Civil War. Scarborough is essentially arguing that Minneapolis could become the defining moment when the political consequences of this administration’s decisions become impossible to reverse.

And voters are feeling the consequences. The Iran War is perhaps one of the clearest examples of the disconnect between Trump’s campaign promises and his governing decisions. Republicans spent considerable time warning voters that a Kamala Harris presidency could drag America into another Middle Eastern conflict. Yet here we are, with Trump overseeing one himself.

According to Axios, Vice President Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff are pushing Trump toward a deal , concerned that restarting the war may not meaningfully improve the situation. Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reportedly want to resume combat .

And Trump has made little effort to hide how he views the political consequences. “I don’t care about the midterms,” he said in May.

The president essentially told voters that the political fallout is not his concern. The midterms are a referendum on the party in power, and while Trump may not personally be on the ballot, the Republicans who were running and plan to run in the future were certainly concerned.

Yesterday, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis appeared on “Straight Shooter” with Stephen A. Smith and told him that Republicans need to start being honest.

“Some of these Republicans, they’re trying to blame Biden for — no, no. Listen, we just got to be honest,” DeSantis said. “Gas is higher. It hurts people, working-class people, and it’s higher because of this conflict. That’s just the fact. If you can’t admit that to voters, then you’re gaslighting them.”

DeSantis is criticizing the messaging and acknowledging that the war is creating real economic consequences for working Americans. And he went further, warning that the conflict could haunt his party down the line: “If it drags on for the rest of his presidency it’s going to be devastating to his ability to get anything done and it is going to be very, very difficult for Republicans in the next cycle.”

This administration has spent considerable political capital defending decisions that are increasingly disconnected from the promises that helped put Republicans in power. The midterm results are a reminder that elections have consequences, even for a president who says he doesn’t care about them. And after a year of controversial decisions, broken expectations and political miscalculations, Trump has created a very expensive bill for his entire party.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.body:
Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) is apparently shrugging off past criticism from Republicans, saying he’s “looking forward” to working with them — even elected officials who have said “mean things” about him.

The Texas Democrat defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general, in their Senate race on Tuesday . Talarico’s win marked the first time a Democrat has won a Texas Senate seat in decades.

Appearing on ABC’s “The View” on Wednesday, he responded to a question about reaching across the aisle following the bitter campaign.

“It made me angry during the election that Republicans unfairly attacked you from every which way,” co-host Joy Behar said.

“All sorts of lies were going around about you, and it was really just mean. Do you still want to work together with these people?” she asked.

“The time for campaigning is over, and the time to lead, the time to serve, is now starting,” he said.

While Behar didn’t reference any specific “mean” remarks, on the campaign trail, Talarico faced attacks on his masculinity, including a “Low-T” nickname. President Trump repeatedly referred to Talarico as “Talafreako” and falsely accused him of being a vegan.

“This is my favorite part of this process. This is when we actually get to solve problems. This is when we actually get to make people’s lives easier and better and less stressful,” Talarico said on “The View.”

“And so I’m looking forward to working with Republicans — including Republicans who said some mean things about me in this race — because that’s my job,” he said.

“My job is to serve. My job is to make this state as good as its promise. And that means I’ll work with anybody and everybody to make that a reality,” Talarico added.

“So I’m going to leave what happened in the campaign in the campaign. I’m now ready to get to work for the people of my state.”

articles.title: Democrats’ election success boosts ranks of Congressional Hispanic Caucus

articles.body:
The Congressional Hispanic Caucus (CHC) will gain more than 10 new members after Democrats’ election night success, boosting the group to its largest membership ever.

“In December, the CHC will celebrate its 50th anniversary with more than 50 incoming Members joining our ranks, making this the largest Congressional Hispanic Caucus in history. This milestone is a testament to the communities, generations of leaders, and advocates who fought to ensure that Latinos have a seat at the table and a voice in shaping our nation’s future,” the caucus said in a Wednesday statement.

While CHC Chair Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.) lost his primary , his district will now be represented by democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier, a Latina woman.

Rep. Darren Soto (D-Fla.), who was in a tight race to retain his Orlando-area district, appears to have pulled out a win and will now lead the CHC.

The caucus also made gains in other races, with Hispanic candidates winning new seats in Texas, California and Nebraska.

In Texas, Tejano music star Bobby Pulido (D) defeated Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R), flipping that seat , while Johnny Garcia (D) defeated her brother Carlos De La Cruz (R) in a nearby district’s race.

President Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement targeting migrants with no criminal history, as well as surging prices, are among the issues attributed to a leftward shift from many Latino voters.

“This election cycle, Latino voters demonstrated their power and influence in shaping the political landscape of this country. We are Americans, and we are America,” the CHC said in its statement.

“Our communities are not an afterthought in our democracy. Our representation is growing, our voices are stronger, and no one can afford to take Latino voters for granted.”
