articles.title: Schumer says Republicans favor ending Iran war immediately, cites ‘power of the purse’
articles.summary: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) said there will be Senate Republican support for ending the war with Iran as soon as possible and threatened that Democrats will use the “power of the purse” to starve the Defense Department of funding if necessary to bring a swift end to the conflict. “We are going to…
articles.body:
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) said there will be Senate Republican support for ending the war with Iran as soon as possible and threatened that Democrats will use the “power of the purse” to starve the Defense Department of funding if necessary to bring a swift end to the conflict.

“We are going to end the war. We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” Schumer said at a press conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) headquarters in Washington on Wednesday.

Four Republican senators voted with Democrats in support of a war powers resolution directing President Trump to withdraw U.S. troops from hostilities against Iran without a formal authorization for use of military force from Congress.

Republican Sens. Thom Tillis (N.C.), Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), and Rand Paul (Ky.) voted to advance the Iran war powers resolution when it last came to the Senate floor.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) was on the fence about how to vote but ultimately voted against the measure in late September after huddling with Senate GOP leaders in the Mansfield Room off the Senate floor.

Cassidy voted in support of an Iran war powers resolution in June and then changed his vote after getting in a shouting match with Trump at a private meeting.

But even if the Senate passes a war powers resolution that has the binding force of law, Trump could still veto it and Democrats don’t have the power to override his opposition.

Democrats have more leverage over Trump’s conduct of the war by blocking funding for the Pentagon.

The White House requested nearly $70 billion in emergency funding for the Pentagon in June, a request that has stalled in the face of intense Democratic opposition.

The annual Defense appropriations bill is also stuck.

Democrats are threatening to block the annual Defense authorization bill and Defense appropriations measure as long as the nation is still at war with Iran.

“My own view is that if the war is over, then the opportunity for bipartisanship on defense authorization and defense appropriations is there. I think if the war’s not over it’s going to be extremely difficult,” Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), the next Senate Democratic whip, told reporters several weeks ago.

images.caption: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee office, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Allison Robbert)

articles.title: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp rejects special session to undercut incoming Bottoms
articles.summary: Outgoing Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp (R) rejected a special session aimed at undercutting incoming Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms (D). “I will not be calling a special session of the Georgia General Assembly in order to curtail executive branch powers or debate redistricting changes,” Kemp wrote in a statement, according to CBS News. “The voters of…
articles.body:
Outgoing Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp (R) rejected a special session aimed at undercutting incoming Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms (D).

“I will not be calling a special session of the Georgia General Assembly in order to curtail executive branch powers or debate redistricting changes,” Kemp wrote in a statement, according to CBS News . “The voters of our state have spoken.”

“As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state,” he continued. But he notably left open the possibility that state lawmakers would need to address Georgia’s finances before January.

This comes after Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson to flip Georgia’s governor’s mansion early into election night. This is the first time a Democrat won the Peach State’s gubernatorial race since 1998, according to the National Governors Association .

Kemp previously scheduled a redistricting session in the state Legislature in June following the Supreme Court gutting a key section of the Voting Rights Act. He urged lawmakers to reconvene to “consider enacting, revising, repealing, or amending general law for the division of the State into appropriate districts” before 2028.

Kemp argued that the high court’s ruling “requires” Georgia to adopt new maps, but it was already too late to redraw for May’s primaries.

It was tabled by Republicans , with Georgia state House Speaker Jon Burns (R) saying that “it was not the right path forward for our state at the time.”

“Changes to our district maps have the potential to impact every voter in Georgia, and they deserve the same thoughtful, fact-driven process that has always guided the House,” Burns said, sharing plans for meetings to hear from voters on the issue.

Though Kemp publicly disagreed with the decision, he stated that redistricting efforts were ultimately the Georgia Legislature’s responsibility.

articles.title: Kiley loses House reelection bid in California
articles.summary: Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-Calif.), who left the Republican Party earlier this year over his opposition to gerrymandering, is projected to lose his reelection bid in California’s newly redrawn 6th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ. Democrat Richard Pan, a physician and former state senator, defeated Kiley by nearly 15 percentage points in a district…
articles.body:
Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-Calif.), who left the Republican Party earlier this year over his opposition to gerrymandering, is projected to lose his reelection bid in California’s newly redrawn 6th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ .

Democrat Richard Pan, a physician and former state senator, defeated Kiley by nearly 15 percentage points in a district reshaped by California’s redistricting effort, ending the congressman’s two terms in the House.

Kiley conceded the race Wednesday, saying he had congratulated Pan on his victory.

“I spoke with Richard Pan and congratulated him on being elected to represent the 6th District,” Kiley wrote on social media early Wednesday. “I’m proud of our campaign and grateful for the amazing support of so many people. Thank you for believing California is worth fighting for.”

Kiley, who currently represents California’s 3rd Congressional District, became one of the most vocal critics of mid-decade redistricting as Republicans and Democrats moved to redraw congressional boundaries ahead of the midterms.

He introduced legislation last year to prohibit the practice nationwide and launched a discharge petition in May to force a House vote on the measure. The effort did not advance.

The redistricting battle escalated after Texas Republicans approved a new congressional map aimed at helping the GOP gain five additional House seats.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) responded by backing Proposition 50, a ballot measure allowing the state to temporarily adopt new congressional boundaries designed to help Democrats, and the measure was approved by voters in November 2025.

Kiley, who was first elected to Congress in 2022 and is a longtime critic of Newsom, opposed the effort, calling gerrymandering a “plague on our democracy” and warned that his existing district would be divided into six pieces.

After the new map was approved, Kiley chose to run in the 6th District, which includes parts of the Sacramento area. The race was an uphill battle for the former Republican, with the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rating the race as “solid Democratic.”

In March, Kiley announced that he was leaving the GOP to become an Independent, citing his opposition to redistricting efforts in both Republican- and Democratic-led states.

Kiley said in September that he would not caucus with House Republicans in the next Congress if reelected and called for changing House rules that require independents to affiliate with a party caucus in order to receive committee assignments.

articles.title: Democratic wins ignite centrist-progressive fight over path to 2028
articles.summary: Democrats emerged from Tuesday’s elections with sweeping victories that gave them control of Congress as well as something they’ve missed since President Trump’s return to the White House: a solid argument that they know what it takes to win. From Texas to Pennsylvania, victories by candidates who appealed to the political middle gave new ammunition…
articles.body:
Democrats emerged from Tuesday’s elections with sweeping victories that gave them control of Congress as well as something they’ve missed since President Trump’s return to the White House: a solid argument that they know what it takes to win.

From Texas to Pennsylvania, victories by candidates who appealed to the political middle gave new ammunition to those who think Democrats need to appeal to people outside their base to reclaim the White House in 2028.

At the same time, the election of progressive Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan offered a counter lesson: that voters could also be willing to get behind candidates running with a liberal ideology.

The results have set the table for a debate over the party’s direction, one that is likely to be waged within the House and Senate caucuses and on the presidential primary debate stage as soon as 2027.

Some Democrats on Wednesday said it’s a welcome debate and that the party should realize it needs both centrists and liberals to win across the country. Limit the infighting, suggest some of these insiders, and learn to work together.

“To win in a lot of places you need a big tent and a big tent needs multiple poles to stand,” said Democratic strategist Eddie Vale. “There is no one magic trick to win elections and we need different types of candidates in different districts and states to win.”

“We need to continue that moving forward instead of fighting over whose group or ideology was the one thing that won it,” Vale added.

But battles over how forcefully to push back on Trump are likely to quickly dominate the conversation.

In particular, Democrats even before the midterms were preparing for debates over investigations into Trump and whether it might lead to impeachment. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is expected to be the Speaker, will also have to deal with these pressures.

“Look, we won. But now the challenge really begins. We can continue the political nonsense of recent years or we can use this time to improve upon our message,” one Democratic strategist said candidly.

“In many ways, people weren’t voting for us Tuesday night, they were voting because they’re pissed off at the status quo,” the strategist said. “They’re pissed off at the establishment. But they still have huge, huge doubts about us. And what we do next is going to matter. If we start pulling the political moves, we’re going to pay in 2028.”

Democratic strategist Basil Smikle agreed, saying Democrats need to “focus on the voter and not Trump” and that lawmakers need to “push policies that improve affordability and stick communities together through their institutions.”

Smikle said Democrats including Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) and Govs. Gavin Newsom of California and Andy Beshear of Kentucky are likely to continue to gain interest in the coming months.

“I think the groundwork has been laid for a new Democratic coalition that only helps whomever emerges in 2028,” Smikle said. “The fact that Democrats also won big in important swing states like Wisconsin, Michigan and Ohio — even in the South with North Carolina and Georgia — suggests that the map for Democrats has expanded greatly from 2024.”

As Democrats dissected Tuesday’s results, the chatter among Democrats was rampant on Wednesday about who might be the best fit to be the nominee in 2028 and what their message might entail.

Some continued to make the case that only a moderate could win nationally. But there were voices in the party who said Tuesday proved otherwise.

Pointing to El-Sayed’s win in Michigan, they said it created a big opening for a candidate like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who is a democratic socialist.

“Aside from the Democrats who won Senate and gubernatorial races in battleground states, AOC was last night’s biggest winner,” said Robert Wolf, a Democratic power broker and former CEO of UBS Americas, using a common nickname for Ocasio-Cortez. “Populism is landing with voters everywhere, and the trends back to Democrats amongst Latino voters helped expand the map to places like Texas and even Florida.”

“This puts her in a great seat to run for the presidency,” said Wolf, who held one of former President Obama’s first fundraisers in New York and quickly got behind his candidacy in 2007.

John Morgan, a longtime Democratic mega-donor, added that if Ocasio-Cortez had the progressive lane to herself, “the others would cannibalize each other … and she is the nominee.”

“America is desperate and hurting,” Morgan said. “That’s when revolutions occur.”

But moderates continued to pound the drum on Thursday that the biggest winners in purple and red states were candidates who appealed to the middle and independents.

“If anyone thinks we’re going to win with a DSA or progressive candidate in 2028, I’ve got a bridge to sell them today,” a second Democratic strategist said, using an abbreviation for the Democratic Socialists of America. “Look at the races one by one. With the exception of Michigan, the Democrats who won statewide appealed to a broad swath of their electorate, full stop.”

The strategist also said the message coming out of the midterms has to be focused exclusively on the economy.

“And we’ve got to do it quickly. We need these two years to show the electorate that we heard what they had to say and we have a plan,” the strategist said. “If we don’t prove that in the next 18 months, it’ll be 2024 all over again.”

But Vale said the biggest lesson of the midterms is that the Democrats need a “big dose of patience and humility about ‘knowing’ who the best candidate will be.”

“Candidate quality mattered a lot this cycle, and we need to let the crucible of the primary play out to see who is going to be the best to emerge,” he said.

images.caption: Democratic Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, left, and Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, right, hold a campaign rally in Austin, Texas, Nov. 2, 2026.

articles.title: Bill Clinton implores Dems to work together ‘with humility and determination’
articles.summary: Former President Clinton released a statement following the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections urging them to work “with humility and determination” to rebuild public trust. “Last night’s victory gives us an opportunity and a responsibility to rebuild trust,” Clinton said in a statement posted to the social platform X on Wednesday afternoon. “We…
articles.body:
Former President Clinton released a statement following the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections urging them to work “with humility and determination” to rebuild public trust.

“Last night’s victory gives us an opportunity and a responsibility to rebuild trust,” Clinton said in a statement posted to the social platform X on Wednesday afternoon. “We should do so with humility and determination, and an open hand, not a clenched fist, to those who didn’t vote for our candidates.”

“I’ve always believed we do better when we work together. Now, the American people have given us another chance to prove it. Let’s make the most of it,” he added.

The Democrats won a Senate majority and are on track to win 54 to 56 seats. The party secured big wins in battleground states like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa, Michigan and Maine. The party also took control of the House and is projected to win around 255 seats, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Candidates made history in states like Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers and became the first Muslim American elected to the upper chamber. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton is going to be the first Democratic senator from the Sunflower State since 1939. In Texas, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) defeated incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott to be elected as the first Latina governor in the state, according to The Dallas Morning News .

“The extraordinary candidates elected last night reflect the diversity of America and the strength of our party,” the former president said in his statement.

In his statement, Clinton alluded to the importance of “helping families with the cost of living and protecting their health care.” Democrats across the country have campaigned on lowering costs.

Recent polls showed that the rising cost of living was a top concern for a lot of voters. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 48 percent of voters ranked cost of living as the most important factor in deciding their vote. A Gallup survey , conducted last month, found nearly half of the respondents marked the economy and healthcare as extremely important factors before casting their ballots.

“The American people have given us clear direction: to put their needs ahead of the chaos and corruption coming out of Washington,” Clinton said.

images.caption: Former President Clinton speaks during the Clinton Global Initiative on Sept. 24, 2025, in New York.

articles.title: Trump: Hegseth would be ‘very popular’ as Tennessee senator
articles.summary: President Trump said Wednesday he is not considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth but predicted the Pentagon chief would be “very popular” if he filled Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s (R-Tenn.) seat. “No, I think he’s doing a very good job,” the president said when asked whether he is considering replacing Hegseth following the Republican Party’s poor…
articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday he is not considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth but predicted the Pentagon chief would be “very popular” if he filled Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s (R-Tenn.) seat.

“No, I think he’s doing a very good job,” the president said when asked whether he is considering replacing Hegseth following the Republican Party’s poor showing during Tuesday’s midterms, where Democrats took the House, the Senate and multiple governors’ mansions.

CBS News reported Wednesday that Trump has been asking advisers and allies whether Hegseth should stay in the post following the midterms.

Hegseth, a former Army National Guard major, is interested in the open Tennessee Senate seat and has been campaigning behind the scenes for the post, The Hill previously reported .

“I think he’s doing a very good job, and I actually think he’d be very popular if he did that. But I haven’t heard that at all,” Trump said Wednesday when asked whether he would want the Defense secretary to fill Blackburn’s seat.

Some political observers agree Hegseth would be a heavyweight in the race.

“I certainly think Pete Hegseth is going to be the guy that is going to have the most weight in the room. I mean, being the Secretary of War and having done what he’s done, and I’m confident [he would be] getting the endorsement of the president, I would think,” Tennessee GOP operative Monty Lankford previously said, using the administration’s preferred name for the Department of Defense.

Questions are swirling inside the Pentagon over how long Hegseth lasts after the midterms even if he is not impeached, something that House Democrats are eager to pursue once they regain the majority, The Hill reported .

Blackburn beat Democrat Jerri Green on Tuesday night to become Tennessee’s first female governor.

Other Tennessee politicians are interested in the Senate seat, which expires in early 2031. Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.), who has campaigned for Blackburn, is in the mix, along with former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs and former CoreCivic CEO Damon Hininger.

“I will be honored to have that,” Rep. Chuck Fleischmann (R-Tenn.), who won his Tennessee’s 3rd Congressional District reelection bid, said in a recent interview with Tennessee Lookout.

“Republicans literally squandered their majority. Congratulations,” he told TMZ DC’s Jacob Wasserman. “We have people losing seats in states that we never thought we’d see, like Ann Wagner lost Missouri. Not that I’m going to cry over that. I might celebrate and go drink some champagne right now. But the point I’m trying to make is, it’s a disaster. It’s a f‑‑‑ing disaster. It’s a full f‑‑‑ing disaster.”

“Imagine if it rained knives for a month and then that turned into a wave. That’s what happened tonight. Ashley Hinson can’t win Iowa. It’s just a s‑‑‑ show,” the former lawmaker expressed, adding that the results “absolutely scares the s‑‑‑ out of” him “for what happens next.”

Santos was referencing Democrat Josh Turek’s defeat of Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) in Iowa’s competitive Senate election. The state has been considered a Republican stronghold, but Hinson’s loss — alongside the GOP’s defeat in the state’s gubernatorial election — has swung it to the Democratic Party.

In Texas, James Talarico became the first member of the Democratic Party to win a Texas Senate seat in decades, defeating state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). Though Republicans held on to seats in Florida, Democrats picked up other key seats in Michigan and Kansas.

In the interview, Santos also withdrew his pitch to become the next White House press secretary, citing Tuesday’s election results.

“I love the president, but no, I’m good,” he said. “Today was a bad night. Everybody has bad nights, and I had a notoriously bad night that everybody saw.”

When asked if he had any advice for incoming congressional members, Santos echoed a post from Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.): “Lawyer up.”

Garcia is also the incoming chair for the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

articles.title: Who won redistricted House seats?
articles.summary: One of the biggest stories of the 2026 midterms came before any votes were cast: the mid-decade redistricting wars. Fearing a backlash to President Trump’s policies at the ballot box, Republicans in several states moved to redraw their congressional maps to shore up their House seats and minimize potential losses. Democrats sought to counter those…
articles.body:
One of the biggest stories of the 2026 midterms came before any votes were cast: the mid-decade redistricting wars . Fearing a backlash to President Trump’s policies at the ballot box, Republicans in several states moved to redraw their congressional maps to shore up their House seats and minimize potential losses. Democrats sought to counter those efforts but ultimately managed just one deliberate redraw of their own in California ahead of Election Day.

After a sweeping victory for Democrats with dozens of gains in the House on Tuesday, how did redistricting efforts hold up around the country?

According to projections from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Republicans picked up just two of the 15 seats they targeted through redistricting. In some cases, the new maps backfired, putting previously safe GOP incumbents at risk.

Here is a review of how the parties’ redrawn maps held up with voters.

Texas was the first state to redraw its lines in 2025, with Republicans aiming to flip at least five Democratic seats.

But the GOP won just one of those redrawn seats: the 32nd Congressional District, where Republican Jace Yarbrough defeated Democrat Dan Barrios by nearly 3 points , according to DDHQ. Trump won the district by nearly 20 points in 2024.

In the 9th Congressional District, which the president won by the same margin two years ago, Democrat Leticia Gutierrez handily defeated Republican Alex Mealer, DDHQ projected. Gutierrez currently leads by 15 points with some votes still left to count.

Republicans’ redistricting gamble in the Lone Star State hinged on Latino voters turning out for the GOP as they did for Trump in 2024. But that support failed to materialize, contributing to defeats for the party in three South Texas districts.

Democratic Reps. Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar both easily held on to their seats in the Rio Grande Valley — the 34th and the 28th Districts, respectively — places which Trump won by more than 10 points each in the last election.

In the battle for the state’s 35th Congressional District , Democrat Johnny Garcia defeated Republican Carlos De La Cruz. De La Cruz’s sister, Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R), also went down to defeat Tuesday night in the 15th Congressional District, falling behind Democrat Bobby Pulido in a seat Republicans did not redraw.

The GOP additionally lost the open 23rd Congressional District, where Democrat Katy Padilla Stout will succeed Rep. Tony Gonzales (R).

On the whole in Texas, Democrats actually left election night with a net gain of one seat, able to counter their redistricting loss with pickups elsewhere.

Florida Republicans also redrew their map , looking to flip four Democratic-held seats. But, as of Wednesday afternoon, it appears they might fall short in all four.

DDHQ projected that Rep. Kathy Castor (D) will hold Florida’s 14th Congressional District, defeating Republican Mike Beltran by more than 5 points . Democrat Pia Dandiya secured a win in the 22nd District, defeating Republican Casey Askar by nearly 4 points.

Plus, in the 25th Congressional District, Rep. Jared Moskowitz bested Republican Scott Singer by nearly 5 points .

The final redrawn district with no winner projected is the 9th Congressional District, where Democratic Rep. Darren Soto leads Republican Dan Green by half a percentage point with nearly all of the vote counted.

Republicans in Ohio also adjusted their congressional lines , but it was not necessarily intentional — they were required by law to do so.

In the process, they made Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur’s 9th Congressional District even more GOP-friendly than it already was and turned Rep. Greg Landsman’s 1st Congressional District into a Trump-won seat.

Kaptur and Landsman both held on, leading their challengers by 5.5 points and 11.5 points, respectively.

And it was Republicans in the Buckeye State who suffered losses — losing the 7th, 10th and 15th Congressional Districts, according to DDHQ projections.

North Carolina Republicans already had a very favorable map but went even further in an attempt to push out Rep. Don Davis (D) in the state’s 1st Congressional District. Despite Trump winning the region by nearly 12 points in 2024, Davis held on by nearly 3 points .

And while maps in other states did not necessarily “backfire” — Republicans still did as good or better under new maps than under old ones — the way lines were drawn in North Carolina nearly created a GOP wipeout Tuesday night.

According to DDHQ projections, Democrats flipped the 6th, 9th, 11th, 13th and 14th Congressional Districts in the Tar Heel State. They are also within 2 points of winning the 3rd, 5th, 7th, 8th and 10th Congressional Districts — all of which remain uncalled as of Wednesday afternoon.

Among the defeated is Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the campaign arm of the House Republicans. Hudson lost to Democrat Richard Ojeda by a 2-point margin .

After the Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais earlier this year — which weakened part of the 1965 Voting Rights Act — Republicans in Alabama and Louisiana redrew maps to each draw out one of their majority Black districts.

In Alabama, Rep. Shomari Figures (D) held on easily in the 2nd Congressional District, leading the GOP candidate by around 7.5 points.

In Louisiana, which held blanket primaries for its House races this year, Democrat Chauna Banks and Republican Blake Miguez will advance to the general election, each with about 19 percent of the vote. That election will be held Dec. 12.

Voters in California approved Proposition 50 in 2025, allowing the state to update its congressional lines to give Democrats five seats in the House — designed as a direct counter to Texas.

Unlike the Texas GOP, however, Democrats in the Golden State were victorious in all five of their redrawn districts, DDHQ projects.

In the 1st Congressional District, Democrat Mike McGuire ousted incumbent Rep. James Gallagher (R) by what is currently a 14-point margin . In the 3rd District, Democratic Rep. Ami Bera — who moved from the 6th District — defeated Republican Robb Tucker and currently leads by the same margin.

In the 22nd Congressional District — a Trump-won district that Democrats aimed to make more favorable — Randy Villegas (D) unseated GOP Rep. David Valadao and leads by a 33-point margin as of Wednesday afternoon.

In the 41st Congressional District, Democrat Rep. Linda Sánchez — who currently represents the 39th District — defeated Republican Mitch Clemmons and led by nearly 30 points.

Finally, in the 48th Congressional District, Democrat Marni von Wilpert notched a win against Republican Jim Desmond and leads by 19 points.

New district lines in Utah were court-ordered by a judge who ruled that the current map — which split Salt Lake City into four Republican seats — was not permitted under the state’s anti-gerrymandering law. The judge ordered a new seat to be drawn that Democrats could win, which they did.

Former Rep. Ben McAdams, who represented the 1st Congressional District from 2019 to 2021, won the open seat , defeating Republican Riley Owen. He currently leads by 47 points.

articles.title: Jeffries taunts Speaker Johnson for saying polls were wrong
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) ribbed Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Wednesday over the Democrats’ landslide midterm victory, saying the GOP leader was right in predicting the polls were wrong — just not in the way Johnson intended. Johnson, heading into Tuesday’s midterms, said repeatedly that the polls forecasting large Democratic gains were simply…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) ribbed Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Wednesday over the Democrats’ landslide midterm victory, saying the GOP leader was right in predicting the polls were wrong — just not in the way Johnson intended.

Johnson, heading into Tuesday’s midterms, said repeatedly that the polls forecasting large Democratic gains were simply inaccurate. He predicted Republicans would keep control of the House despite the seemingly long odds.

After Tuesday’s rout, Jeffries offered Johnson a sideways commendation.

“Mike Johnson was correct. The polls were wrong,” Jeffries said during a press conference in Washington. “It wasn’t simply a blue wave; it was an American tsunami.”

As of Wednesday afternoon, Democrats had flipped dozens of Republican seats without losing a single battleground incumbent of their own, putting them on track to control at least 255 seats in the next Congress. The results stunned even Democrats, and the margins will provide Jeffries, who’s in line to replace Johnson as Speaker, with a comfortable cushion to move his party’s legislative priorities next year.

Jeffries on Wednesday offered a rough outline of what those priorities will be, echoing the legislative changes Democrats had promised voters on the campaign trail this year. The list features aggressive steps to tackle the high cost of living, including efforts to expand ObamaCare subsidies, reverse Republican Medicaid cuts, roll back President Trump’s tariffs and end the Iran war, which has led to a spike in global fuel costs.

“The American people have chosen the economy over extremism,” Jeffries said. “The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction, and that’s exactly what House Democrats will deliver on Day One.”

Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), who’s expected to become the Democratic whip in the next Congress, went a step further, saying voters gave Democrats a “mandate” to enact their change agenda, particularly when it comes to the economy.

“Democrats promised a new path forward, and last night, the voters delivered a mandate for it,” he said.

Aside from the affordability message, Democratic leaders are also promising aggressive investigations into allegations of corruption within the administration, including a closer examination of the Trump policies that have boosted the personal finances of the president and his family.

Jeffries on Wednesday dismissed the idea, however, that Democrats would impeach the president, as some liberals want to do.

“I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment,” he said. “We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability, and on accountability.”

Jeffries worked with Trump during the president’s first term on a package of criminal justice reforms, which marked a rare episode of bipartisan cooperation under Trump. It’s unclear if such compromises will be possible in the president’s second term, during which the clash between the parties has grown only more heated.

Jeffries said neither he nor Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) has spoken with Trump since midterm voters gave Democrats the majorities in both chambers. But he emphasized that he’s willing to work with anyone, as long as there’s a shared goal of helping Americans navigate volatile times.

“That begins with decisively addressing the affordability crisis,” he said.

articles.title: Trump touts ‘magnificent’ ballroom in first remarks after midterm drubbing
articles.summary: President Trump, in his first public remarks since Republicans lost big in the midterm elections, showed off the White House ballroom construction Wednesday. The president signed the final beam, along with workers and other officials, and watched it get lifted into place. He didn’t mention the results of the midterm elections until taking questions from…
articles.body:
President Trump, in his first public remarks since Republicans lost big in the midterm elections , showed off the White House ballroom construction Wednesday.

The president signed the final beam, along with workers and other officials, and watched it get lifted into place. He didn’t mention the results of the midterm elections until taking questions from reporters, when he also remarked on Vice President Vance’s statement that the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms.

Trump called the ballroom “the most powerful building structurally … they say ever built and it was designed that way so the president can have safety,” Trump said. “It’s been the dream of presidents to have a ballroom for 150 years.”

He said it is ahead of schedule and under budget, which he has said many times.

“When I get criticized, like, ‘Why are you working on the White House?’ I’m doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America,” he said. “And it’s got to be pristine. It’s got to be perfect. And if you take a look at it, that’s what it is right now.”

“Just this whole magnificent space will be a very important space in the future life of our country,” he said.

He also talked about the planned Triumphal Arch, the new helipad on the White House’s North Lawn, the planned National Garden of American Heroes and his renovation of the East Potomac Golf Links.

When asked about Vance’s statement on social platform X, Trump said, “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term.”

He said he thought the war was “worth it.”

“I mean, well, you have no choice,” he said.

The midterm elections came out in the Democrats’ favor, flipping seats to take control of both the House and Senate.

He said he would “get along probably” with the Democrats “unless they want to be destructive.”

“But I have the power of the veto,” he said, adding that he has already spoken with some Democrats.

He said he would “stay out of” the race to pick a new House Republican leader after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he would not run .

articles.title: Young voters appear to move away from Republicans: Survey
articles.summary: Young voters appeared to distance themselves from Republicans in this year’s midterm election blowout for Democrats, according to a new poll. In The AP Voter Poll, which surveyed 2026 midterm voters, 73 percent of voters aged 18 to 29 backed a Democrat for their House seat, while 25 percent of the age group backed a…
articles.body:
Young voters appeared to distance themselves from Republicans in this year’s midterm election blowout for Democrats, according to a new poll.

In The AP Voter Poll , which surveyed 2026 midterm voters, 73 percent of voters aged 18 to 29 backed a Democrat for their House seat, while 25 percent of the age group backed a Republican.

According to The Associated Press , which partnered with SSRS for the poll, the age group was about evenly divided between President Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

Fourteen percent of those who backed a Democrat for their House seat were aged 18 to 29, while 6 percent of those who backed a Republican for their House seat were in the same age group.

The congressional map on Tuesday was painted blue, with the Democrats locking down both the House and Senate majorities and securing a chance to restrict Trump’s power until the end of his second term.

The Democrats’ victories came amid a challenging political environment for the GOP, with Republicans weighed down by issues including the unpopular war in Iran, Trump’s slumping approval numbers and concerns about the cost of living.

Democrats are projected to end up with 261 seats in the House and 55 seats in the Senate , according to Decision Desk HQ, marking gains for the party that currently holds 214 seats in the lower chamber and 47 seats in the upper.

The success for Democrats on Election Day is a far cry from where the party was in the wake of the 2024 election, an era that was marked by infighting, soul-searching and frustration.

The AP Voter Poll took place between Oct. 19 and Nov. 3, featuring 81,290 voters and a margin of error of 0.5 percentage points.

articles.title: What to know about the 5 Mamdani-backed measures New Yorkers are projected to pass
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) secured key wins on Election Day with several ballot proposals that would build upon his administration’s efforts to expand housing, outdoor dining and public safety projects in the city. All five measures are expected to succeed, according to projections from The Associated Press. “Tonight, New Yorkers voted for…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) secured key wins on Election Day with several ballot proposals that would build upon his administration’s efforts to expand housing, outdoor dining and public safety projects in the city.

All five measures are expected to succeed, according to projections from The Associated Press.

“Tonight, New Yorkers voted for a government that moves as fast as they do,” Mamdani said in a Tuesday evening statement shared by his office.

“From opening outdoor dining faster to speeding up street safety projects to accelerating housing production, we are cutting red tape that will directly address the affordability crisis and help New Yorkers stay in the city they love,” the Democratic mayor continued. “Now comes the work of turning these votes into results.”

Here’s what to know about the five ballot proposals.

The first measure would simplify the process for installing ramps, planters and sidewalk cafes in the city.

Under this amendment, public hearings are no longer required to approve these additions, and the City Council can no longer vote to reject an approved permit for a sidewalk cafe. The public would still have an opportunity to weigh in on these public use issues through an online portal process.

The measure would shorten the outdoor dining application process from around eight months to two months, according to an estimate from the mayor’s office.

NYC Hospitality Alliance, a trade association advocating for restaurants and bars in the city, celebrated the amendment’s passage as “a welcome step toward opening outdoor cafes sooner” in a statement shared Wednesday on the social platform X.

The ballot proposal was opposed by watchdog group Common Cause, which cited concerns with a loss of public input on these additions.

“Streamlining administrative processes should not mean removing meaningful opportunities for New Yorkers and their elected representatives to weigh in on decisions affecting public spaces,” the group said in a statement ahead of the election.

The Center for Independence of the Disabled, New York also expressed concerns that a reliance on written comments would create a “barrier to participation” for certain groups, including people with sensory or digital access limitations.

Contracting process for small businesses and nonprofits

This amendment proposal seeks to simplify steps currently mandated for vendors seeking contract approvals from New York City’s Procurement Policy Board.

The measure would reduce the required paperwork for vendors by simplifying the contractor questionnaire and removing mandatory hearings and the board’s quarterly meetings.

The city estimates changing the contractor questionnaire could save up to 30 days in the contracting process and take a burden off of city agencies for annual reporting requirements.

Common Cause supported the ballot proposal, lauding it for “reducing unnecessary administrative burdens” to boost support for small businesses and nonprofits.

Proposal 3 is a three-pronged amendment aimed at streamlining street construction projects, the transfer of unused city property and office leasing.

The proposal would permit the city’s transportation department to begin construction without consulting other city agencies, allow the sale of lots smaller than 10,000 square feet without City Council approval and lift hearing and approval requirements for the acquisition of new office space for city employees.

Fiscal watchdog group Citizens Budget Commission (CBC) supported the amendment , saying it would provide a needed acceleration for these initiatives. The change could speed up street safety projects, including bike lanes, by at least 33 percent, according to the mayor’s office.

Critics cited concerns with the amendment’s provisions related to the sale of public land. The Municipal Art Society of New York urged New Yorkers to vote no on the measure in October, arguing it would permit the sale or transfer of “valuable public land and development rights without sufficient safeguards.”

The fourth proposal seeks to streamline the process by which contractors apply for construction permits by creating a centralized online permitting hub. Under this amendment, the Department of Buildings (DOB) would have until 2030 to implement this new online platform.

Additionally, the measure would move the approval process for waterfront structure permits under the DOB and allow these permits to be approved at a faster pace.

This ballot proposal drew support from the CBC, Common Cause and pro-housing group Abundance New York.

Nonpartisan civic education coalition D9 Harlem Votes opposed the measure, expressing skepticism about how effectively the community will be able to weigh in on construction proposals through this new online portal.

The final ballot measure approved by New Yorkers on Tuesday creates a new savings goal for the city’s reserve funds, including its rainy day fund, to strengthen long-term financial planning.

The city would set a new target of 12 percent of the previous year’s total tax revenue, with the reserve fund goal methodology being updated every four years.

The measure was opposed by the CBC , which called this goal insufficient and said it would “enshrine the failing status quo in policy.”

Common Cause supported the target, noting this amendment would establish “clearer rules for maintaining and accessing financial reserves” and “strengthen accountability across administrations.”

articles.title: Christie: Vance ‘will be remembered’ for backing controversial Ramaswamy ad
articles.summary: Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) on Tuesday said Vice President Vance “will be remembered” for backing former Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad featuring Gov.-elect Amy Acton’s (D) mother. “JD Vance will be remembered for standing behind Vivek and his ad,” Christie wrote on social media Wednesday. “A man who wrote a…
articles.body:
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) on Tuesday said Vice President Vance “will be remembered” for backing former Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad featuring Gov.-elect Amy Acton’s (D) mother.

“JD Vance will be remembered for standing behind Vivek and his ad,” Christie wrote on social media Wednesday. “A man who wrote a book about Catholicism. It’s a disgrace.”

Christie attached to the post his broader analysis on the Ohio race’s outcome when asked by ABC’s David Muir on Tuesday night.

“Well look, you not only have to question the judgment of a man who would take a woman, an elderly woman, out of the car she was living in, in a parking lot of a church in Pennsylvania with her cats and put her in front of a video camera and make that a TV ad in a gubernatorial race,” he said.

Christie said the “real problem going forward” was Vance standing up for Ramaswamy “100 percent … not only as a person and a candidate, but he stood behind that ad.”

“And Vivek Ramaswamy will be forgotten. He is going to be sent to the dustbin of history,” the New Jersey Republican added before giving his evaluation on Vance and what he thinks the vice president will be remembered for.

Acton won 52.31 percent of the vote, according to The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ as of 3:04 p.m. EST on Wednesday. Ramaswamy received 44.4 percent of the vote.

She will become Ohio’s first Democrat elected to be governor in roughly 15 years, and the first woman elected as governor in Buckeye State history. She served in Gov. Mike DeWine’s (R) administration as the director of the Ohio Department of Health. DeWine will leave office, as he is term limited.

Vance slammed Republicans last month who criticized Ramaswamy’s ad, which featured Acton’s mother accusing her daughter of being a “liar” and saying Acton “needs help.”

The vice president said Ramaswamy ran an ad that “calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” and urged voters to focus on “the substance and focus on the facts.”

“I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance said at a fraud task force press conference.

President Trump also defended the ad , telling Ramaswamy that he “should keep it up.”

Conservative commentator Scott Jennings said last month that Vance could have “ignored” the ad and said that not all of Ramaswamy’s surrogates needed to agree with the campaign’s decisionmaking.

“This issue of whining, I took some issue with that today, because I don’t see people whining about this, I think they are warning about this,” he added.

articles.title: Romney counts reasons GOP lost: ‘Bad policy, bad character’
articles.summary: Former Sen. Mitt Romney (R-Utah) on Wednesday listed off reasons he thought his party failed in this year’s midterms, in which Democrats won both the House and Senate. “Bad policy, bad character make bad politics: erratic tariffs, impulsive Iran war, blanket pardons, apparent corruption, weaponized justice, ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] brutality, mountainous deficits, hiding…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Mitt Romney (R-Utah) on Wednesday listed off reasons he thought his party failed in this year’s midterms, in which Democrats won both the House and Senate.

“Bad policy, bad character make bad politics: erratic tariffs, impulsive Iran war, blanket pardons, apparent corruption, weaponized justice, ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] brutality, mountainous deficits, hiding [Jeffrey] Epstein, abandoning allies and coddling enemies,” Romney said in a Wednesday afternoon post on the social platform X.

“Hoping for a course correction, for the country and for my party,” he added.

Romney, who made his own presidential bid in 2012, has historically been a critic of President Trump. He was also the lone GOP senator to vote to convict Trump in both of his impeachment proceedings.

In their quest to hold on to the House and Senate this year, Republicans faced hurdles like the unpopular war in Iran, concerns about the cost of living and Trump’s approval rating. However, the congressional map went blue Tuesday, with Democrats taking both congressional chambers.

Democrats are projected to end up with 261 seats in the House , according to Decision Desk HQ, up from their current total of 214. In the Senate, they’re projected to finish with 55 seats, up from the 47 they have in the 119th Congress .

Romney wasn’t the only Republican critic of his party in the wake of the 2026 midterm returns. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) said in a Tuesday night post on X that the midterm blowout by Democrats was “about holding Republicans accountable for betraying their promises.”

“Tonight’s outcome isn’t about placing faith in Democrats or socialist principles; it’s about holding Republicans accountable for betraying their promises,” Massie said on X.

“All Republicans had to do was: 1. put Americans First 2. not start another war 3. prosecute sex traffickers,” he added.

Troy Nehls (R-Texas), according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Trever Nehls won the district’s Republican primary by a landslide and faced Democratic opponent Marquette Greene-Scott in a…
articles.body:
Texas Republican House candidate Trever Nehls is projected to win his race for the Lone Star State’s 22nd District and replace his twin brother, Rep. Troy Nehls (R-Texas), according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Trever Nehls won the district’s Republican primary by a landslide and faced Democratic opponent Marquette Greene-Scott in a solid Republican district. Trever Nehls garnered about 52 percent of the vote while Greene-Scott notched 48 percent, with more than 95 percent of the vote reported as of Wednesday afternoon.

Trever Nehls is a retired U.S. Army colonel who first enlisted in 1988. He later commanded service members in Iraq and Afghanistan. He was recognized for his service with three Bronze Stars and the Combat Action Badge.

He previously served as constable for Fort Bend County Precinct 4 from 2013-20. He also ran his own company, Nehls Consulting LLC.

President Trump endorsed Trever Nehls last December , not long after Troy Nehls announced his retirement . He praised the Nehls brothers for being “fierce advocates” for the MAGA movement.

A wave of prominent elected Republicans backed Trever Nehls, including House Speaker Mike Johnson (La.), House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (La.), Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick.

Troy Nehls told constituents he chose to retire to focus on his family “after conversations with my beautiful bride and my girls.” He said he spoke with Trump before making the decision.

articles.title: Boyle bows out on challenging Fetterman in 2028
articles.summary: Newly reelected Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) said Wednesday he does not plan to challenge Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) for his Senate seat in 2028. Boyle thanked supporters for reelecting him Tuesday night in a Facebook post. The Hill’s election forecasting partner Decision Desk HQ projected he had won 80.78 percent of voters’ support as of…
articles.body:
Newly reelected Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) said Wednesday he does not plan to challenge Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) for his Senate seat in 2028.

Boyle thanked supporters for reelecting him Tuesday night in a Facebook post. The Hill’s election forecasting partner Decision Desk HQ projected he had won 80.78 percent of voters’ support as of 3:25 p.m. EST on Wednesday, with 80 percent of votes counted. His opponent, Republican Jessica Arriaga, claimed 19.22 percent of the Pennsylvania electorate.

“For months, many of my supporters have urged me to consider running for US Senate in 2028,” he wrote. “I have always said that after the November 2026 election, I would make a decision based on one simple question: where can I have the biggest impact on public policy?”

“After months of consulting many people, including current senators and past committee chairs, it is quite clear that I can have a much bigger impact as House Budget Committee Chairman than as a freshman member of the Senate,” he continued. “Therefore, I will not be running for the Senate.”

Boyle, who previously served as the House Budget Committee’s top Democrat, will become its chair in January now that his party has reclaimed the lower chamber. He said he hopes to use his elevated status to “finally get this nation’s fiscal health back on track,” “bring more resources back home” and “fight for economic policies that finally help working Americans.”

The Pennsylvania Democrat previously chose to forego a bid to run for the Senate when Sen. Pat Toomey (R-Pa.) opted not to seek another term. Boyle said in April 2021 he considered his family when deciding against a statewide campaign.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) in September said he “might” challenge Fetterman in the 2028 primary, though he said his focus was on helping House candidates in the lead-up to Tuesday’s elections. He suggested he would “deal with 2028 when we get past” the midterms.

“John Fetterman’s nowhere to be seen on the campaign trail,” Deluzio told host Chris Stirewalt on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday” in September. “And again, to be very blunt, I don’t think there’s any Democrat in Pennsylvania who wants him campaigning with them, even if he would show up.”

Fetterman has defended his party affiliation despite straying from Democrats on key issues and facing backlash from supporters over his support for Israel. Democrats blasted him in September after he made a video appearance boosting his fellow Pennsylvania senator, the GOP’s Dave McCormick, at the Republican National Committee’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas.

He told reporters at the time he was not considering switching parties, later saying if he became a Republican, “ then I’ll be a liar .”

But the Pennsylvania senator remains critical of his party’s turn against Israel and defends the country’s military campaign in Gaza. Fetterman said in July his party abandoning the country’s Middle Eastern ally would be a red line.

“If our party ever becomes — and just makes it official — the anti-Israel party, that’s when I would leave ,” he told The Hill’s Alexander Bolton at the Hill Nation Summit.

articles.title: Cornyn says GOP ‘forgot how to win’ under Trump
articles.summary: Outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R) issued his own analysis Wednesday after the GOP suffered major losses across the country and in the Lone Star State in Tuesday’s midterms. The four-term senator reflected on the party’s defeat in an op-ed published in The Wall Street Journal, titled “Republicans Forgot How to Win Elections.” “This week’s…
articles.body:
Outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R) issued his own analysis Wednesday after the GOP suffered major losses across the country and in the Lone Star State in Tuesday’s midterms.

The four-term senator reflected on the party’s defeat in an op-ed published in The Wall Street Journal, titled “Republicans Forgot How to Win Elections.”

“This week’s beat-down wasn’t only foreseeable, it was foreseen,” the Republican wrote.

Cornyn, who lost his seat in the Texas Republican Senate primary runoff to state Attorney General Ken Paxton, said the party failed to satisfy “four basic rules of coalition politics” this election cycle.

He outlined the key tenets as broad voter appeal, candidate likeability, promise delivery and integrity.

On his first point about electoral appeal, the senator noted that “successful coalitions add, they don’t subtract.” He pointed to the GOP’s 2024 wins among white working-class voters, Latino men and Black voters.

“This year, losing candidates like Ken Paxton and Mike Collins shrank the tent, obsessing over ‘RINOs’ and political theater,” he wrote.

Cornyn also cited GOP candidate Bo French’s loss in the Texas railroad commissioner race . The Republican nominee lost the support of some within his party, after GOP lawmakers like Cornyn accused him of engaging in “blatant bigotry” against college students of South Asian descent.

More broadly, the Texas senator said the GOP suffered from a deficit in likeable candidates and said the party has engaged in a “strange reverse personality test” that favors performance over authenticity.

“This is a losing mindset that Republicans must outgrow,” Cornyn said, adding, “It selects for nominees who can’t win general elections.”

The senator cited the Trump administration’s failures to deliver on his 2024 campaign promises to bring down rising costs and boost employment opportunities. President Trump’s approval rating has taken a hit amid rising fuel costs and inflation during the Iran war and his administration’s trade fight with Canada.

“Americans elected the Donald Trump who put on the apron of the Golden Arches and got a plan for a Triumphal Arch instead,” Cornyn wrote.

Lastly, the GOP senator expressed shortcomings in character and integrity among Republican candidates this election cycle.

“Voters won’t trust Republicans to cut fraud and scams out of government programs until we cut them out of our own ranks,” he wrote.

Cornyn alluded to his primary race against Paxton in Texas but did not mention the attorney general by name. Paxton has faced a series of controversies during his time in state leadership related to his personal conduct and felony security fraud indictments.

“When Republicans force voters to choose between policy and personal character, it is unfair to them and suicidal for us,” he wrote. “Here in Texas, traditional conservatives and independents were asked to swallow an almost comical list of personal scandals and improprieties.”

Despite Tuesday’s losses, Cornyn wrote that he remains “optimistic” about his party’s ability to chart a successful political future.

“We know what the American people want because they showed us: a big-tent Republican Party, competent, focused on Americans’ daily concerns, with room for traditional conservatives and MAGA supporters alike,” the senator wrote.

“That is the path back to a governing majority in 2028,” he continued. “Anyone who is willing to turn the page, restore integrity and rebuild our party can count me in.”

articles.title: Democrats flip legislatures, clinch trifectas in key states
articles.summary: Democrats from New Hampshire to Wisconsin are on track to make massive inroads in state legislatures across the country, as the party racks up wins up and down the ballot. The party is poised to flip both state legislative chambers in at least two states and clinch trifectas in at least five states so far.…
articles.body:
Democrats from New Hampshire to Wisconsin are on track to make massive inroads in state legislatures across the country, as the party racks up wins up and down the ballot.

The party is poised to flip both state legislative chambers in at least two states and clinch trifectas in at least five states so far. Democrats are also set to gain ground in red territory, cracking GOP trifectas in places like Georgia, North Carolina and Texas.

As of Wednesday, the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee (DLCC) said the party is on track to flip at least a dozen state Houses and Senates as results continue to trickle in. Decision Desk HQ has yet to formally project many of these races.

Democrats are already touting these victories as another way to check President Trump and his agenda, with the party also clinching control of the House and Senate in Washington, D.C.

Here’s a look at the states where Democrats look set to flip legislative chambers, gain trifectas and even make inroads:

Capitols clinched in New Hampshire, Wisconsin

Democrats are poised to make their biggest gains in New Hampshire and Wisconsin, flipping the full legislatures.

State Navigate forecasts that Democrats are favored to win 253 seats in the New Hampshire House while Republicans hold on to 147. The nonpartisan state government elections tracker forecasts that Democrats and Republicans are so far favored to win 12 seats each.

The Associated Press has not called majorities for either chamber in the Granite State yet, though some news outlets have declared both a win for Democrats.

Democrats will still have to contend with a Republican governor, with Kelly Ayotte sailing to reelection Tuesday.

The party also made record gains in the Badger State. The Associated Press projects that Democrats will hold an 18-15 edge in the Senate and a 53-46 majority in the state Assembly.

The party was buoyed in large part by recent electoral wins on the Wisconsin Supreme Court, which in 2023 paved the way for a redraw of the state’s legislative maps. That decision helped usher in a more competitive map for both parties, giving Democrats new areas to compete in.

Republicans blamed their poor performance Tuesday on the bleak political landscape for the GOP, Democratic investment in state legislature races and the impact of top-of-the-ticket races.

“With the 2028 elections and the next round of congressional redistricting approaching, Republicans must confront the challenges ahead and make a sustained commitment to winning back and defending our majorities,” Republican State Leadership Committee President Edith Jorge-Tuñón said in a statement.

At least five states are set to have Democrats at the helm of their state legislatures and governor’s mansions.

Minnesota was widely seen as Democrats’ best chance for a trifecta. Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) is set to become the state’s next governor, besting state House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R).

The party is projected to expand its majority in the state Senate and clinch the state House to end the state’s divided government under outgoing Gov. Tim Walz (D). Though votes are still being counted, the AP projected Democrats winning both chambers, notching at least 35 seats in the state Senate and 73 in the state House. The party last held a trifecta in 2024.

In Michigan, Democrats are also projected to flip the state House, ending Republicans’ 58-52 advantage, according to the AP . Democrat Jocelyn Benson is also set to succeed outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D), while Democrats are projected to win at least 22 state Senate and 60 state House seats. The party currently holds a 20-18 edge in the state Senate.

Democrats also notched trifectas in battleground Nevada and Pennsylvania.

Democrat Aaron Ford ousted Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo in Nevada, while Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro easily won reelection Tuesday . Democrats are projected by the AP to hold their majority in the Nevada state Legislature, while the party is set to flip the Keystone State’s upper chamber to clinch a trifecta. Pennsylvania last had a Democratic trifecta in 1993, according to Ballotpedia .

In the Midwest, Wisconsin Democrats are on track to win their first trifecta since 2010.

Democrat David Crowley won the election to succeed Gov. Tony Evers (D), while their party is poised to capture the majorities in both legislative chambers, according to the AP.

“By flipping hundreds of seats and the largest number of chambers in a single night for Democrats since the 1980s, we have put Democrats in a stronger position all across the map,” DLCC President Heather Williams said in a statement.

“Our victories have shattered Republicans’ grip on our statehouses, and with two years left in the Trump administration, it is clear that voters trust Democratic state legislators to both stand as a bulwark against Republicans’ MAGA agenda and to fight on their behalf to make progress, lower costs, and invest in their communities,” she added.

Democrats are also on track to make serious inroads in red-leaning states.

In Arizona, the final tally of votes is still up in the air, but Democrats could deliver a trifecta after Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs won a second term Tuesday.

The AP projects that the party is set to clinch enough seats to at least tie the state’s upper chamber, and no call has been made for either party in the state House. Republicans currently control both chambers.

On the other side of the country, the AP projects that North Carolina Democrats will win control of the state House. The outlet has yet to project the upper chamber.

Democrats also cracked Republicans’ trifecta in Georgia for the first time since 2004 after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson for the governor’s mansion .

The party looks poised to crack the GOP’s supermajority in the state Senate, while the party could be in striking distance of flipping the state House.

In Texas, Democrats are projected to flip the Texas House alongside Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s successful gubernatorial bid to end Republican control in the state.

Democrats broke GOP trifectas in Ohio and Iowa, too, and the party is set to possibly bring about an end to Republican supermajorities in states like South Carolina and Kansas as the final votes are tallied.

articles.title: Polls saw the Democratic wave. Here’s why they missed the tsunami
articles.summary: The polls had a decent night Tuesday in predicting Democratic wins but fell short of projecting the blue tsunami that ultimately swept larger-than-expected Democratic majorities into power in the House and Senate. Democrats exceeded even their own expectations on election night, winning Senate races in states such as Kansas and South Carolina, along with contested…
articles.body:
The polls had a decent night Tuesday in predicting Democratic wins but fell short of projecting the blue tsunami that ultimately swept larger-than-expected Democratic majorities into power in the House and Senate.

Democrats exceeded even their own expectations on election night, winning Senate races in states such as Kansas and South Carolina, along with contested House races across the country.

Polling widely suggested ahead of Election Day that a blue wave could be coming, as Democrats led or were at least competitive in all battlegrounds they were focused on flipping.

But the polls underestimated the extent of just how much Democrats would dominate the midterms.

That’s a far cry from what has felt like the norm since President Trump’s first election in 2016.

“What we did get is a 2020-level polling miss, thereabouts, but the inverse where the Democrats were underestimated in polling,” said Chaz Nuttycombe, the executive director of State Navigate.

Nuttycombe pointed to a couple factors to explain what happened. Chiefly, he pointed to how pollsters weigh their results.

Instead of simply polling respondents and presenting those results as their finding, pollsters use weighting to project what they expect the electorate to look like in an election, based on certain key demographics like education, race and party identification.

Ahead of the election, State Navigate put together a report expressing that polls might be underestimating Democrats. Nuttycombe said many pollsters weighted their results based on expecting an electorate similar to 2022, when former President Biden was in office.

He said looking at the 2018 electorate, the first midterm year for Trump, was a better parallel.

Nuttycombe also pointed to an issue with total recall bias, when results are impacted by flaws in how respondents reported they voted in a past election.

“You had a whole bunch of people who were lying, who are definitely Trump voters who said that they weren’t,” he said.

When voters either choose to lie to a pollster about who they voted for, or potentially don’t remember correctly, it can skew results when it comes to weighting a poll. Fewer people who reported voting for Trump in 2024 may cause a pollster to believe those voters are being undercounted.

Nuttycombe dismissed the idea of people being ashamed of their vote but instead pointed to voter frustration with the president, illustrated by Trump’s low approval rating.

“This is them being frustrated and them saying in their vote choice, ‘I did not vote for this. I’m p—ed off, and I’m going to go vote,’” he said. “Mostly, these people are voting for Democrats.”

In terms of the bottom-line results on who won, the polls certainly pointed in the right direction.

The final average from The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ, which aggregates surveys from across nonpartisan, left-leaning and right-leaning professional pollsters, showed Democratic candidates ahead in most of the key Senate races. They led by varying margins in Georgia, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas — all of which the Democratic candidate won.

Even Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina led narrowly by 0.1 point in the average over Sen. Darline Graham (R) based on the limited public polling available.

The average also showed Democrat Mary Peltola leading by 1.4 points. She is locked in a close race with Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) as the final ballots in Alaska’s Senate race are tallied.

But margins were underestimated almost across the board, with significant implications for gubernatorial and downballot races.

Some of the largest overperformers of the night included Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) in Georgia, who won by 18 points despite a 10-point lead in the average, and James Talarico (D) in Texas, who led Republican opponent Ken Paxton by nearly 12 points despite holding just a 3.5-point lead in the average which is a gap within the margin of error for most polls.

Democrats also pulled off impressive wins in gubernatorial races.

In arguably the most notable flip of the evening, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) lost his reelection bid to state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D), who led by 7 points. The polling average showed Abbott ahead by 1.3 points, well within the margin of error but still didn’t indicate Hinojosa could win so comfortably.

In another example, Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs (D) led on average in polling by just under 7 points, but she’s currently ahead by 13 points.

Still, pollsters did have some successes from the results, as many outcomes at least signaled most states that were seriously in contention so the public had an idea of where they should pay attention.

Alec Tyson, the senior vice president and lead pollster for Ipsos, argued that polls did well in illustrating “the arc of the election.” There’s more to evaluating the electorate that’s coming than just the horserace polls that often dominate people’s attention as Election Day approaches.

“A lot of things were true for the past decade in politics until they weren’t this year, and one of the things polls did a good job of is documenting the erosion of Trump’s approval,” he said.

Tyson said many observers and pollsters for years have seen Trump as having a low ceiling and a high floor for his approval rating, keeping it in a narrow range that often stayed in the mid-to-low 40s. Polls effectively showed just how much Trump’s approval had dropped over the past year, a major indicator that a clear rebuke of the president was coming.

They also showed that the cost of living was the top issue on voters’ minds as inflation remained high. They showed Democrats taking the lead in the question of who voters trust more to handle the economy — a striking change that hadn’t been observed in more than a decade .

“It’s worth noting that the average of the generic ballot, even going into election night, was saying this has a chance to be a historic night,” Tyson said.

RealClearPolitics showed Democrats’ lead in the generic ballot to be 8.8 points, larger than any midterm cycle since 2006 , another major Democratic wave.

Tyson acknowledged pollsters still have more to learn and will need to adjust based on the new information of this year, just as they have during past cycles when Trump outperformed.

“Direction polls did a great job painting or kind of outlining the story of the election, and even so, we have much to learn,” he said. “And I think we’re wise to assess each election on its own context and see what we can learn and carry forward.”

articles.body:
Conservative commentator Scott Jennings on Tuesday called the GOP’s losses in the 2026 midterms a “country a‑‑ whooping.”

“Well, look, I’m not going to sugarcoat it. There’s a political science term for what’s happening. It’s called a country a‑‑ whooping. That’s what’s happening right now, across the board,” Jennings said on CNN Tuesday night.

“Look, you know, there’s a lot of reasons for what’s happening right now. The most immediate issue is cost of living and gas prices, and that is the bottom line,” he added. “You could read into a lot of other things. You can be jubilant about this, that, or the other. But at the end of the day, the American people have here and now concerns, and that’s really the lesson you got to take away from this.”

Democrats locked down both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, most likely stymieing President Trump’s policy agenda for the next two years.

Republicans faced an uphill battle this election cycle amid Trump’s slumping approval rating, the unpopularity of the war in Iran and cost-of-living concerns.

According to a polling average from The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 38.4 percent Wednesday evening, with his disapproval rating at 58.7 percent.

Democrats are projected to go from 47 seats in their Senate caucus to 55, according to DDHQ , and from 214 seats in the House to 261. They also notched victories in states like Texas and Kansas, which have historically leaned red.

articles.title: Haley Stevens triples down on Rogers endorsement after El-Sayed’s victory
articles.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) on Wednesday tripled down on her endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed took victory after a bitter midterm battle on the campaign trail. Rogers lost to El-Sayed, receiving 45.48 percent of the vote to El-Sayed’s 52.52 percent, according to The Hill’s election partner Decision…
articles.body:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) on Wednesday tripled down on her endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed took victory after a bitter midterm battle on the campaign trail.

Rogers lost to El-Sayed , receiving 45.48 percent of the vote to El-Sayed’s 52.52 percent, according to The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ as of 1:15 p.m. EST on Wednesday.

Stevens began a lengthy post on the social platform X stating that her beliefs were “never measured by who would win at the ballot box” and that she recognized that her “decision has consequences.”

“All important decisions do,” she continued. “I don’t regret it, but I am truly sorry that it upset some of my colleagues and people I care about personally.”

Stevens addressed her “unwavering” support for Israel — a point of contention during her failed primary fight against El-Sayed — and said she backed a U.S. ally “that is imperfect and in need of some political reforms of its own.”

“As co-chair of the House caucus on antisemitism, endorsing a man who stood with Hasan Piker and his antisemitic bile was always a tough fit for me,” she said, referring to the left-wing political commentator and Twitch streamer. “But I’ve been taught my whole political life that at the end of an election, you come together and support the winner, and I hoped I could help him moderate. Instead, he got worse.”

“I regret my original endorsement, because I could have spared the country and my family from these past few days and from attempts to find a cause for an action that is consistent with a lifetime of my beliefs,” she said. “The endorsement was the outlier act. Rescinding it was not.”

The Michigan Democrat noted that those “colleagues who know me best understood that this was never easy for me,” calling her original endorsement for El-Sayed “highly unusual.” She said that as a “student of history,” she chose to stick with what she believed “mattered more.”

“What mattered more was truth over political convenience,” Stevens wrote. “Nothing about this experience has been easy on me or those closest to me. I was elected to do a job, and I am going to finish it. I was elected as a Democrat, and I still believe our party should be big enough for more than one viewpoint. I will keep fighting antisemitism wherever it shows up, in either party, for as long as I am in public life.”

The post concluded with a congratulations “to everyone who won” and a call to continue talks on “how we build tolerance from viewpoints and embrace one another, especially when we disagree.”

Stevens stunned Democratic colleagues with her endorsement of Rogers just two days before the midterms, with members of her staff resigning shortly after .

She defended her decision Sunday night in a tense interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper, which fellow Democratic Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell called “one of the most painful interviews I’ve ever watched.” Stevens defended her pick once again on Tuesday, telling The Hill’s broadcast partner NewsNation that it was “absolutely” worth it.
