articles.title: All the GOP House incumbents swept away in the blue wave
articles.summary: Democrats had a historic night Tuesday, sweeping both chambers of Congress and making gains deep into Republican territory. The party won nearly everywhere it was expected to and in places people never thought it had a chance. As of Wednesday afternoon, 27 House incumbents had been projected to lose their seats by Decision Desk HQ…
articles.body:
Democrats had a historic night Tuesday , sweeping both chambers of Congress and making gains deep into Republican territory .

The party won nearly everywhere it was expected to and in places people never thought it had a chance. As of Wednesday afternoon, 27 House incumbents had been projected to lose their seats by Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), and eight more were trailing in the count with no projection.

No state was a greater source of shock and defeat for Republicans than North Carolina, where the party has already lost five seats — one of them open — and trails in another.

Rep. Brad Knott (R) lost to Democrat Paul Barringer in North Carolina’s 13th Congressional District . In the 14th Congressional District, Rep. Tim Moore (R) lost to Democrat LaKesha Womack. Democrats flipped the 6th Congressional District as well, with Rep. Addison McDowell (R) losing to Democrat Cyril Jefferson. And in the 9th Congressional District , the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, Rep. Richard Hudson, lost to Democrat Richard Ojeda. Each defeat was by 2 points or just higher.

In all four of those races, Democrats had less than a 25 percent chance of winning in DDHQ’s preelection forecast.

In the 5th Congressional District, Rep. Virginia Foxx trails by just 99 votes to Democrat Chuck Hubbard. DDHQ has not projected a winner in that race.

Pennsylvania Republicans also had a rough go of it as four incumbents were defeated.

Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R) lost to Democrat Bob Brooks in the 7th Congressional District by a 13-point margin. Just north of the 7th District, Democrat Paige Cognetti defeated Rep. Rob Bresnahan in the 8th District by just less than 9 points . Both Mackenzie and Bresnahan won their seats in 2024.

Two incumbents who have resisted waves before also fell to defeat. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R), a moderate member who sometimes publicly disagrees with President Trump, lost to Democrat Bob Harvie in the 1st Congressional District . And in the Harrisburg area, Rep. Scott Perry (R) — a former Freedom Caucus chair who voted not to certify the election in 2020 — lost to Democrat Janelle Stelson by a 10-point margin .

Just across the Delaware River, two incumbents lost in New Jersey. Rep. Tom Kean Jr., a Republican who was absent from the House for months without explanation, lost to Democrat Rebecca Bennett by nearly 16 points . Kean ultimately revealed he had depression. And in South Jersey, Rep. Jeff Van Drew was defeated by Democrat Zack Mullock in a big upset . Van Drew initially flipped a GOP-held seat in 2018 as a Democrat but switched parties in 2019 .

In New York’s Hudson Valley, Rep. Mike Lawler (R) trails Democrat Cait Conley in the 17th Congressional District, though DDHQ has not called the race. A ballot scanning issue in a key county in the district delayed counting Tuesday. Lawler, though, has conceded .

In Virginia, Rep. Jen Kiggans (R) lost to former Rep. Elaine Luria (D) by nearly 9 points in the 2nd Congressional District. Kiggans beat Luria back in 2022 but faced headwinds amid the Iran war in the military-dominated district. And in the 1st Congressional District, Democrat Shannon Taylor defeated Rep. Rob Wittman by just more than 1 point.

Democrats in Ohio had a strong night , winning the marquee statewide races and defeating three House incumbents. Rep. Max Miller (R) lost to Democrat Brian Poindexter in the 7th Congressional District by nearly 10 points. Miller’s campaign was blown up by allegations of domestic abuse against his daughter and ex-wife, who happens to be the daughter of Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno (R).

Rep. Mike Turner (R), a moderate congressman in the 10th Congressional District, lost to Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker by just less than 2 points . In the neighboring 15th Congressional District , Rep. Mike Carey lost to Democrat Don Leonard by more than 6 points.

Just north in Michigan, one Republican incumbent was defeated and another one trails. Rep. Tom Barrett lost reelection to Democrat William Lawrence in the 7th Congressional District by just more than 3 points. In the 4th Congressional District, Rep. Bill Huizenga (R) trails Democrat Sean McCann by a little less than 2 points, but DDHQ has not yet projected a winner.

Wisconsin Democrats defeated two GOP incumbents, in the 1st and 3rd congressional districts. In the 3rd District , Rep. Derrick Van Orden lost to Democrat Rebecca Cooke by just more than 6 points. Rep. Bryan Steil lost to Democrat Mitchell Berman in the 1st District by nearly 4 points .

Two Republican incumbents lost in Iowa: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in the 1st Congressional District and Rep. Zach Nunn in the 3rd Congressional District. Miller-Meeks, who won election to Congress by just six votes in 2020, lost to Democrat Christina Bohannan — their third time facing each other — by more than 9 points . Nunn lost to Democrat Sarah Garriott by 7 points.

In Missouri’s 2nd Congressional District , Rep. Ann Wagner lost to Democrat Fred Wellman by nearly 5 points. Missouri Republicans attempted to redraw the maps but were stopped last minute from doing so by a court decision, putting the 2nd District back on the map.

The suburban Indianapolis 5th Congressional District changed hands as well, with Rep. Victoria Spartz losing to Democrat J.D. Ford by more than 3 points.

In South Texas, Rep. Monica De La Cruz lost to Democrat Bobby Pulido by more than 22 points in the state’s 15th Congressional District. Trump won the 15th District by nearly 20 points in 2024, marking a huge shift to the Democrats in the heavily Latino district.

In Arizona, Democrats defeated one GOP incumbent with Rep. Juan Ciscomani’s loss to Democrat JoAnna Mendoza in the 6th Congressional District. Rep. Eli Crane (R) also trails Democrat Jonathan Nez in the 2nd Congressional District, though DDHQ has not called the race.

California Democrats successfully defeated two incumbents using their redrawn map , a response to a gerrymander passed by Texas Republicans. In the 1st Congressional District , Rep. James Gallagher lost to Democrat Mike McGuire, and in the 22nd Congressional District , Rep. David Valadao lost to Democrat Randy Villegas.

Only one incumbent has lost so far in Colorado, but that number has the potential to grow. Rep. Gabe Evans lost reelection to Democrat Manny Rutinel in the 8th Congressional District , but Reps. Lauren Boebert and Jeff Crank both trail their Democratic challengers in the 4th and 5th congressional districts, respectively. Boebert nearly lost in the 3rd Congressional District in 2022, and moved to the 4th District , which was thought to be a safer district for her to run in.

Some potential upsets brewing — but where DDHQ has not yet called a winner — come in Minnesota and Tennessee. In Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District, Rep. Brad Finstad (R) trails his Democratic opponent, Jake Johnson, by less than 500 votes. And in Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District, Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R) trails Democrat Victoria Broderick by fewer than 300 votes in a district Trump won by nearly 25 points in 2024. DDHQ’s preelection forecast gave Broderick just a 3 percent chance of winning.

DDHQ makes a projection in a race when it has greater than 99 percent certainty of the call. Late arriving mail ballots or provisional ballots could shift the final margins in the closest races.

articles.title: Appeals court rules for Mamdani on pied-à-terre tax, reversing lower court
articles.summary: An appeals court ruled in favor of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s (D) pied-à-terre tax, which would place an annual surcharge on certain second homes. This reverses a lower court decision that found Mamdani’s Finance Department violated the plaintiffs’ due process rights through its method of determining who would pay the tax on second…
articles.body:
An appeals court ruled in favor of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s (D) pied-à-terre tax, which would place an annual surcharge on certain second homes.

This reverses a lower court decision that found Mamdani’s Finance Department violated the plaintiffs’ due process rights through its method of determining who would pay the tax on second homes worth more than $5 million.

The tax was proposed by Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) in April, but it has faced numerous legal challenges ever since. The pair said at the time that the tax would help narrow the city’s budget deficit and would be an annual surcharge on one- to three-family homes, condominiums and co-ops owned by people who have a separate primary residence.

This lawsuit did not concern the legality of the tax but rather the notices the Finance Department sent to around 17,000 residents in the city, alerting them they were subject to the tax. The plaintiffs, a group of New York homeowners, previously argued they were not given enough time to prove if they did or didn’t qualify for the tax.

“From day one, those with the most have attempted to use every legal avenue available to shield their wealth and avoid contributing more to our city,” Mamdani wrote in a statement. “We are heartened by the Appellate Division’s ruling in the City’s favor, and we will continue working with our partners in Albany to defend this law against the ongoing challenges in Suffolk County.”

“Our commitment has not changed. We will implement the pied-a-terre surcharge fairly and efficiently, ensuring that those most able to contribute do their part to build a city that works for everyone,” he concluded.

Randy Mastro, the first deputy mayor of New York City under former Mayor Eric Adams (D), slammed Mamdani’s administration rollout of the tax, calling it “admittedly botched” in a statement to The Hill.

“The court today took the procedural offramp of standing to avoid addressing the merits of this case,” Mastro said. “To be clear, though, the ultimate day of reckoning for this ‘pied-a-terre’ surcharge will occur next month when its constitutionality will be decided. We remain confident we will prevail and put an end to this unconstitutional surcharge altogether.”

Mamdani said in July that the tax was to provide the city with needed “long-term solutions” to its fiscal challenges.

articles.title: Trump faces reckoning, but focuses on ballroom, after devastating losses
articles.summary: President Trump’s legacy is facing a moment of reckoning following sweeping Democratic wins in the House and the Senate that will impact the trajectory of the last two years of his presidency. Despite his efforts to mobilize his normally loyal political base, the coalition that sent Trump to the White House in 2024 fell apart…
articles.body:
President Trump’s legacy is facing a moment of reckoning following sweeping Democratic wins in the House and the Senate that will impact the trajectory of the last two years of his presidency.

Despite his efforts to mobilize his normally loyal political base, the coalition that sent Trump to the White House in 2024 fell apart Tuesday evening. The result was nationwide Democratic wins including in red strongholds like South Carolina and Texas.

Trump argued his party underperformed because he was not on the ballot, but many Republicans say the losses are indicative of the president’s loosening grip on the party.

“It’s definitely going to leave a mark,” said Marc Short, Trump’s former legislative director during his first administration, referring to Tuesday’s massive Republican defeats.

“I think other presidents have had significant midterm defeats and have still had a strong historical record, but I think there’s no doubt it was a pretty clear and loud repudiation of what the last two years have been.”

Additionally, Republicans warn that Democratic majorities in the House and the Senate could pose a major roadblock for the president’s agenda.

As of Wednesday evening, Democrats had a 54-44 majority over Republicans in the Senate, while Democrats led Republicans 249-153 seats in the House.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), whose state narrowly avoided the blue wave, offered a dire assessment of his party’s future during a press conference Wednesday.

“This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans,” DeSantis said.

DeSantis predicted in Tuesday night social media post that the chances of confirming a conservative successor to Supreme Court Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, if they stepped down in the next two years, would be “zero.” The governor argued that those chances would remain low during a “hypothetical GOP admin” in 2029 because the party would not be able to win enough seats in the Senate.

In his first public appearance after the landslide, Trump spent most of his time talking about the details of his under-construction ballroom. The president signed the last beam installed in the structure, in what his Interior secretary called a celebratory day.

The president also discussed his beautification projects at the White House and around Washington, D.C.

“I’m doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America. It’s got to be pristine. It’s got to be perfect,” Trump said.

The president took several questions from reporters on the midterms, the Iran war, and working with Democrats in the new Congress. However, he kept returning his focus to the construction site.

Wednesday’s event marked the second time this week Trump delivered remarks to talk about his beautification projects in Washington. On the Monday before Election Day, the president delivered remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to talk about renovations.

“This rout makes clear that a legacy is not built with ballrooms and gilded vanity projects — in fact, they send the opposite message to hardworking Americans,” said John Ullyot, former deputy assistant to Trump during his first administration and author of “The President Deserves Better.”

“To forge a true legacy in his final two years, Trump should replace his cadre of yes-men with competent leaders who aren’t afraid to give frank advice and help him work across the aisle to get important things done,” he continued.

Ullyot was moved out of a communications role in the Pentagon early this year.

Trump appeared to rule out a Cabinet shake-up in an interview with Fox News on Tuesday, saying the midterm election losses did not have anything to do with his Cabinet secretaries.

“I’ve been doing a lot of great things for a long time,” he said. “It’s just a point in time. Just a point in time. Just the way it is. There was a mood in the air, I guess.”

In a statement to The Hill, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Trump’s Cabinet would continue working to deliver his agenda.

“As the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,” she said.

Ahead of the midterms, questions swirled about potential staff and Cabinet shake-ups if the GOP lost big, which is not unusual in administrations after a poor midterm performance.

“Obama lost nearly as badly in 2010, and it doesn’t seem to have tarnished his [legacy]. Trump has 2 years to work on his legacy. Not nearly as long as Obama (who had 6, including a successful 2012 re-elect) but still time,” said Mick Mulvaney, Trump’s former chief of staff during his first administration.

Short said he was unsure whether Republicans had reached “the low point” yet.

“There’s a lot of healing that we have to do and there could be even more divisions inside of our team about the pathway forward,” he said. “I’m probably not thinking it’s going to boomerang around as quickly as 2028 for us.”

articles.title: Progressive group calls for Senate Dems to replace Schumer as leader
articles.summary: The progressive group Indivisible called for Democratic lawmakers on Wednesday to replace Sen. Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) as Democratic leader after the party secured control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. “Yesterday, voters made it very clear that they want a new generation of Democratic fighters,” the group wrote in a social media…
articles.body:
The progressive group Indivisible called for Democratic lawmakers on Wednesday to replace Sen. Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) as Democratic leader after the party secured control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

“Yesterday, voters made it very clear that they want a new generation of Democratic fighters,” the group wrote in a social media post . “We need a leader in the Senate who is capable of leading that fight. It’s time for Senate Democrats to choose new leadership.”

The group cited the Democratic leader’s faltering approval ratings in its Wednesday statement. An NBC News poll conducted at the end of October found only 13 percent of registered voters viewed Schumer’s leadership positively.

“The American people did not elect Democrats by historic margins just to bend the knee and go back to business as usual,” Indivisible said in its statement. “Senate Democrats need to listen to the voters and turn the page on status quo politics.”

During a speech Wednesday morning, Schumer celebrated the Democrats’ wins in Senate races as “a generational remake of the Senate map that has huge consequences for history.”

Unfortunately for Schumer, it could also portend bleak consequences for his own future in Democratic leadership.

Newly elected Senate Democrats in Michigan , Kansas , Illinois and Maine have all publicly stated they would not back Schumer as majority leader next term.

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) told Louisiana-based magazine Current Affairs in May that Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) was his “number one pick for majority leader.”

At a campaign rally in July after the Maryland senator endorsed him , El-Sayed introduced Van Hollen as the “ next Senate majority leader .”

Other new Democratic senators have stayed quiet on how they might cast their votes in the upcoming leadership fight.

Sen.-elect James Talarico (D), who pulled off a major victory for his party in the Texas Senate race, declined to commit to supporting Schumer for majority leader in a September interview with Punchbowl News , telling the outlet his party needs “new blood” in Washington.

Similarly, New Hampshire Rep. Chris Pappas (D), who won the state’s open Senate race Tuesday, declined to commit to backing Schumer in a September interview with MS NOW’s Peter Alexander. He emphasized a need for “new voices in leadership.”

articles.body:
Democrats won big on Election Day. Prediction markets gave an early glimpse

A dominant performance by Democrats in the midterm elections created a political earthquake, shifting the balance of power in Washington, D.C. But most of Tuesday’s results were foretold in the hours before polls closed by online prediction markets .

Platforms, like Kalshi and Polymarket , have proven capable in recent election cycles of providing an increasingly accurate view into the public’s perception of likely political outcomes and current events.

They performed with impressive accuracy again on Tuesday, as traders poured billions of dollars into election markets at a time when the platforms face growing scrutiny from lawmakers about the dangers of insider trading and gambling addiction.

“There’s no way around it, the prediction markets seem to be highly accurate,” said Ross Dahlke, an expert in computational social sciences and a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

“The markets just react so quickly to new information in a way that a lot of traditional media isn’t set up to do, particularly with their concern over accuracy, fact-checking — for better or for worse,” he added.

Democrats were expected to perform well on Tuesday, given widespread voter concern about the economy and war with Iran.

But the volume of trading on prediction markets this election cycle and the speed with which the platforms were able to correctly predict races was notable.

Many of Tuesday’s key race results were being projected accurately on prediction market platforms hours before major TV networks, which use decision desk data and voter analysis to make race calls, declared winners.

Kalshi, one of the nation’s most widely used prediction market platforms, said Wednesday its markets had correctly predicted 98 percent of House, Senate, governor, attorney general, lieutenant governor and secretary of state races.

The company said it compared market favorites at 5 p.m. EST shortly before the first polls closed in Indiana and Kentucky to races that have been called so far.

articles.summary: Presented by AstraZeneca {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story Democrats get their health agenda ready ahead of takeover Reinstating the Affordable Care Act’s enhanced premium tax credits, reversing the Trump administration’s Medicaid cuts and even making progress toward Medicare for All are on the table as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in…
articles.body:
Democrats get their health agenda ready ahead of takeover

Reinstating the Affordable Care Act’s enhanced premium tax credits, reversing the Trump administration’s Medicaid cuts and even making progress toward Medicare for All are on the table as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January.

While ObamaCare tax credits and Medicaid will be low hanging fruit in the party’s legislative agenda, Democratic leaders will have to navigate tensions between progressives itching to pursue Medicare for All and moderates who want more incremental change.

“We’re going to fight hard to make sure that we can ensure that every single American can afford to go see a doctor when they need one,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), likely to be the next House speaker, said during a victory speech Tuesday.

“We will fight for your hospitals. We will fight for your nursing home. We will fight for your community-based health clinics. And we’re going to fight to reverse these painful Medicaid cuts.”

But without a 60-vote, filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, passing legislation following through on pledges to lower costs will be difficult. In addition, attempts to roll back or even delay President Trump’s sweeping Medicaid cuts will likely be met with a veto from the White House — if it gets that far.

Still, Americans are facing a health care affordability crisis , and Democrats recognize a need to go bold to fix it. Some new Democratic Senate winners from election night, such as Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Maine’s Troy Jackson, are supporters of Medicare for All.

When it became evident Tuesday night Democrats were headed for a major takeover, Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) wrote on social media, “WHO WANTS MEDICARE FOR ALL?”

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Finance Committee, said in a statement his panel “will create a new foundation for America’s health care system that Democrats get their health agenda ready ahead of takeover , gives Americans cheaper and better health care, and ends the corporate chokehold on our nation’s health care system.”

In the House, Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.) launched a bid to chair the powerful Energy and Commerce Committee.

“Democrats must relentlessly pursue an agenda that puts working people first and focuses on resolving the outrageous price increases that are making it impossible for families to make ends meet,” Pallone said in a statement. “Over the last two years, Republicans have driven up the cost of virtually everything and imposed the largest health care cuts in history – stripping health care from millions, forcing people to pay more for less, and shuttering hospitals.”

Pallone also pledged to advance policies that lower costs and “expand access to quality and affordable health care.”

articles.summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Wednesday said “deportations will continue” in a social media post following Democrats’ sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections, claiming both the House and Senate. Democrats campaigned against President Trump’s immigration crackdown, with some using the call to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as a slogan on the…
articles.body:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Wednesday said “deportations will continue” in a social media post following Democrats’ sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections, claiming both the House and Senate.

Democrats campaigned against President Trump’s immigration crackdown, with some using the call to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as a slogan on the campaign trail.

Mullin challenged those calls and other criticism toward the agency, including in the lead-up to the midterms. He clapped back at former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton after she warned that ICE officers could try to intimidate voters at the polls, questioning why she was “still relevant.”

“Even in my confirmation hearing, this was brought up, and I made it very clear that ICE agents aren’t going to be around polling places unless there’s a threat,” Mullin told Fox News host Will Cain before polling closed Tuesday.

Democrats have vowed to use their power in Congress to restrain ICE and could withhold future funding, as well as be an authority to conduct oversight on the agency. But they will likely face resistance from Republican lawmakers and attempts at the legislative level could face a presidential veto, which Trump has assured before and after the midterms .

Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) introduced a bill last month, the “Reimagining Safety Act,” to overhaul U.S. immigration agencies, which included replacing the Department of Homeland Security with a “community-centered” department.

The ICE critic, a member of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that the deaths of those detained by ICE and Customs and Border Protection, and of those deported by the U.S. were the “reason DHS must be dismantled and something new must take its place,” she said last month.

Ahead of the midterms, a New York Times/Siena University poll found that 52 percent of likely voters backed Democrats on handling immigration over Republicans, with 45 percent saying they backed Republicans.
